Post-wildfire mass movements in Vouraikos Gorge
papers.summary: Wildfires and landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards worldwide, causing severe environmental degradation, human casualties, and major economic losses. In recent decades, post-wildfire geomorphic hazards have gained increasing scientific attention due to their strong association with soil erosion, debris flows, and slope instabilities. Wildfires significantly alter vegetation cover, soil structure, and hydrological response, thereby increasing the susceptibility of steep terrains to earthflows and landslides. These secondary hazards often persist for years after a fire event, threatening infrastructure, ecosystems, and human life. This study investigates the occurrence of post-wildfire earthflows and landslides within a recently burned area in Western Greece. The research focuses on identifying the environmental and geomorphological factors that contributed to repeated slope failures following a major wildfire event. To achieve this objective, remote sensing data were integrated with topographic, hydrological, climatological, geological, vegetation, and field survey data within a Geographic Information System (GIS) environment. Multi-source geospatial analysis was employed to examine terrain characteristics, drainage conditions, vegetation recovery, and slope instability patterns in the affected area.

papers.title: Regional-scale SBAS-InSAR characterization and susceptibility-oriented assessment of recurrent landslide activity in Tizi Ouzou, Algeria
papers.summary: This study presents a regional-scale analysis of recurrent landslide activity in Tizi Ouzou, northern Algeria, using Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR time-series data integrated with a susceptibility-oriented assessment. The study area is characterized by mountainous terrain and recurrent slope instability affecting several sectors, including Aïn El Hammam and Yakouren. Ascending and descending Sentinel-1 acquisitions from January 2023 to January 2026 were processed using a Small Baseline Subset (SBAS) workflow to derive line-of-sight (LOS) velocity and temporal coherence indicators for regional deformation analysis. The results show generally high temporal coherence in both geometries, with median values of 0.90 for the ascending data and 0.87 for the descending data, supporting a reliable interpretation of spatial deformation patterns. LOS velocity distributions are centered near zero, indicating that a large part of the area is stable or only slowly deforming. However, localized anomalies reach approximately -5.8 to +4.7cm/yr, revealing spatially clustered deformation hotspots consistent with recurrent slope instability. To strengthen the interpretation of deformation signals, the InSAR-derived indicators are analyzed together with conditioning factors such as topography, geology, hydrology, land cover, and infrastructure. This integrated framework supports hotspot mapping, comparative evaluation of deformation patterns across affected sectors, and regional susceptibility assessment. The study provides a systematic characterization of recurrent landslide activity and demonstrates a scalable and transferable approach for combining SBAS-InSAR products with susceptibility analysis in data-scarce, landslide-prone mountainous environments.

papers.title: Monitoring critical infrastructure and our hazardous planet with satellite radar
papers.summary: Satellite radar interferometry is transforming our ability to detect and monitor subtle ground and structural motion over remarkably different scales, from individual assets to entire tectonic plate boundaries. In this plenary, I will explain how interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) works and why it has become such a powerful tool for both infrastructure monitoring and understanding our hazardous planet. I will show how open-access satellite missions, from Sentinel-1 to NISAR, are making routine, high-resolution deformation monitoring possible over our entire planet. I will present examples spanning practical industrial applications and large-scale geophysical science: monitoring rail and road networks, dams, and mines; tracking landslides and volcanic unrest worldwide; and measuring deformation associated with earthquakes and long-term tectonic processes across regions such as the Tibetan Plateau. I will also discuss how radar wavelength, resolution, and revisit time determine what can be measured and where. I will conclude by looking ahead to a rapidly expanding satellite ecosystem, including publicly and privately funded missions, and what these developments mean for our ability to live safely on our hazardous planet.

papers.title: Space-Air-Ground Integrated Approach for Landslide Identification and Characterization in High-Altitude Mountainous Regions: A Case Study in Shannan, Xizang, Himalayas
papers.summary: Geological hazard investigation in high-altitude mountainous regions is challenging due to complex terrain, limited accessibility, and the need to identify potential hazards over large areas while characterizing their local features. This study develops and applies a sequential, multi-scale space–air–ground workflow integrating Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR, UAV photogrammetry, airborne LiDAR, and field investigations in Shannan, Xizang, China. Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR analysis identified 65 deformation anomaly areas covering a total of 139 km2. Based on a comparison with existing geological records and field surveys, eight landslide sites were identified as new discoveries. UAV and LiDAR techniques were subsequently employed, together with field investigations, to examine the identified anomalies and characterize their topographic and geomorphological features. Integrated hazard model maps were completed for 20 geological hazard sites, and two representative cases were selected for detailed analysis: the slowly creeping landslide in Cuodui Village and the rockfall at Mawujue Temple. These cases illustrate the need to interpret deformation signals in conjunction with hazard type, terrain characteristics, and field evidence. The results highlight the practical value of integrating satellite-based deformation monitoring, high-resolution three-dimensional terrain characterization, and field investigations within a coherent workflow for geological hazard identification and characterization. The workflow provides a practical reference for investigations in comparable high-altitude mountainous regions, although its transferability depends on local terrain conditions and data availability, and its effectiveness in identifying previously unrecorded hazards requires further validation.

papers.title: A Producer-Led Product-Consistency Audit of an AHP Landslide-Susceptibility Raster: A Philippine Road-Corridor Case Study
papers.summary: An acceptable analytic hierarchy process (AHP) consistency ratio measures the coherence of pairwise judgement, not the integrity of a geographic information system (GIS) product. This study audits three relationships in a relative landslide-susceptibility index for the 22.14-km Villa Verde Road corridor, Pangasinan, Philippines: raster-pair and partition consistency, regenerated-overlay encoding and coverage, and factor-score rule consistency. Comparison of the retained slope surface with the former slope-score raster identified 12 cells incorrectly assigned score 4 despite slopes of 25.16°–29.69°. Correcting them changed 12 index values and, with re-derived class breaks, 20 class labels (0.85%). A separate aspect comparison found 1,167 of 2,357 cells (49.51%) differed between the retained raw-derived surface and adopted V1 scores; the raw-derived alternative changed 307 cells under fixed thresholds and 301 after re-derived Jenks breaks. Weight sensitivity tests produced up to 533 changed cells in one-at-a-time scenarios, while mean Dirichlet agreement ranged from 75.43% to 87.27%; Very High-class Jaccard overlap was lower (0.60–0.77). These first-party checks and conditional sensitivity results do not constitute independent workflow, source-data or predictive validation. The derivative-processing cause and intended aspect convention remain unresolved; principal results are conditional on V1.

papers.title: Seismic evidence for a two-stage origin of the October 2026 Budhi Gandaki landslide in the Nepal Himalaya
papers.summary: On 10 October 2026 a rock avalanche left the south face of the Chamar massif, Nepal, ran 8.7 km down the Ungilung and dammed the Shyar above the Budhi Gandaki. Single-force inversions of one regional and 28 teleseismic records resolve four force pulses 23–26 s apart, alternating westward and eastward. Flow simulations released from the face favor two stages of failure, a smaller one at the onset of the high-frequency signal and the main body 40–60 s later, together 6–21 Mm3, reaching the Shyar in three minutes.

Unsupervised landslide detection across heterogeneous environments: a terrain-constrained object-based extension of the SLIP algorithm using PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 imagery
papers.summary: Rapid mapping of rainfall-induced landslides remains difficult in heterogeneous and vegetated terrain, particularly where flooding, channel erosion, and sediment redistribution produce spectrally similar disturbances. We present Object-Based SLIP (OB-SLIP), a terrain-constrained extension of the Sudden Landslide Identification Product for training-free landslide-candidate mapping. The framework combines robust changes in NDVI, NDRE, red and near-infrared reflectance, and brightness with object filtering and slope constraints. Four ablations were evaluated: U0 (spectral baseline), U1 (spectral + objects), U2 (spectral + terrain), and U3 (spectral + objects + terrain), with two Random Forest benchmarks in Italy. In the 2022 Southern Misa River Basin case, U0 achieved 0.599 recall, U1 reduced candidate objects from 24,876 to 4,146, and U3 produced the strongest false-positive suppression. On a common held-out region, U3 reached F1 = 0.185, closely followed by U1 at 0.182, compared with 0.130–0.133 for the Random Forest benchmarks. In the 2019 Cyclone Idai transfer, U0 detected 85.86% of 2504 evaluable initiation points within 20 m. U2 reduced candidate area by 15.34% without measurable point-hit loss, whereas U3 reduced it by 59.05% relative to U0. The Italy-derived object and terrain rules were transferred without Zimbabwe-reference tuning. Results show that OB-SLIP provides a transparent screening framework in which object and terrain constraints reduce candidate burden, but their contribution depends on landscape context and sensor resolution.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal prediction of reservoir landslide deformation by coupling multi-orbit InSAR with a hydrometeorology-modulated deep learning model
papers.summary: Reservoir impoundment and water-level fluctuations often reactivate slow-moving landslides, but reliable three-dimensional deformation prediction remains difficult at the hillslope scale. This is mainly because single-orbit InSAR line-of-sight measurements cannot reveal true downslope kinematics or hydrologically driven processes. We investigated two landslides, L1 (Xiapingzi) and L2 (Maocaofang), in the Baihetan Reservoir area, China. Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 InSAR from ascending and descending orbits was combined with a Surface Parallel Flow (SPF) model to reconstruct slope-aligned displacement. Using these deformation fields, we developed a Feature-wise Linear Modulation-based Convolutional Gated Recurrent Unit (FiLM-ConvGRU), coupling ConvGRU-based spatiotemporal learning with precipitation and reservoir water-level conditioning. Lagged dependence analysis revealed site-dependent associations: L1 showed stronger and more consistent relationships with reservoir water-level fluctuations, while L2 showed weaker and more heterogeneous responses, with characteristic lags of 0–24 days. The FiLM-ConvGRU achieved PCC values of 0.871 and 0.735 and R2 values of 0.732 and 0.490 for L1 and L2, respectively. Compared with ConvGRU, PCC increased from 0.858 to 0.871 for L1 and from 0.691 to 0.735 for L2, indicating site-dependent predictive information from environmental conditioning. These results show that integrating multi-orbit InSAR, terrain-constrained displacement retrieval, and hydrometeorology-conditioned deep learning provides a route for short-term full-field deformation forecasting of reservoir landslides.

papers.title: Evaluating the application of clustering analysis on seismic data: an example from Western Quebec Seismic Zone
papers.summary: Abstract. Clustering analysis can identify statistically significant spatial groupings within geoscience data (including earthquakes, landslides, volcanoes and wildfires), providing insight into potential mechanisms influencing the patterns. Previously, the DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) algorithm has been successfully applied in highly active seismic regions to investigate spatial patterns associated with earthquake processes. However, its application is often limited to a small (or a singular) exploration of DBSCANs governing parameters. To demonstrate the capabilities of clustering analysis, here we apply DBSCAN to a large earthquake dataset in a complex intraplate seismic region. For 40 years of earthquakes within Canada's active intraplate Western Quebec Seismic Zone (WQSZ), we explore the full range of input variables to understand the sensitivity of the algorithm to creating cluster scenarios. By evaluating 70+ clustering scenarios generated through different parameter combinations, the results demonstrate that DBSCAN can provide significantly different patterns and therefore a wide range of interpretations. Our finding here is that caution is required when using and interpreting clustering analysis and that a clustering algorithm alone is insufficient for determining the most geologically representative spatial patterns within the region. However, when integrated with temporal analyses and available geological information, DBSCAN-derived clusters identify spatial patterns associated with tectonic features. Specifically, the results show that seismicity within the WQSZ may be influenced by the reactivation of ancient crustal structures inherited from past tectonic events. This study shows the challenges when relying on a small range of clustering analysis input combinations for interpretation, and highlights the importance of evaluating a broad range of parameters when exploring large geoscientific datasets.

papers.title: Adaptive GNSS/InSAR Fusion for Three-Dimensional Deformation Reconstruction and Mass-Conservation-Based Thickness Inversion of Reservoir Landslides
papers.summary: Three-dimensional (3D) deformation monitoring of reservoir landslides remains challenging because InSAR observations have limited sensitivity to motion parallel to the satellite flight direction, vegetation-related decorrelation can reduce the availability of coherent measurements, and GNSS stations are often sparse. This study presents a GNSS/InSAR fusion framework for reconstructing 3D surface deformation and estimating landslide thickness. Ascending- and descending-track Sentinel-1 line-of-sight (LOS) deformation measurements are combined with three-dimensional GNSS observations in a joint observation model. A landslide-mask-constrained first-order Tikhonov regularization is used to constrain spatial differences within the mapped landslide, while a benchmark-anchored Helmert variance component estimation (VCE) strategy adaptively updates the relative weights of the ascending- and descending-track InSAR observations, with GNSS observations retained as the reference group. The reconstructed mean velocity field is then used in a mass-conservation-based thickness inversion that accounts for surface-slope advection and combines Laplacian regularization with borehole soft constraints, assuming an approximately stationary basal sliding surface. Synthetic experiments indicate that the framework improves reconstruction stability and recovers the northward component under the tested sparse-GNSS configuration. In the Hongyanzi case study, the northward deformation component yielded an RMSE below 6.5 mm yr−1 when compared with the GNSS observations used as inversion constraints; this is an in-sample residual measure rather than independent validation. At the seven boreholes incorporated as soft constraints, the final thickness field yielded an in-sample RMSE of 0.545 m and absolute residuals of approximately 0.20–0.78 m. papers.title: Landslide susceptibility over the Tibetan Plateau in a warming climate
papers.summary: Introduction The Tibetan Plateau (TP) is experiencing increasingly frequent landslides under climate warming. Projecting landslide susceptibility across the TP requires joint representation of antecedent rainfall, soil wetness and temperature under changing climate conditions. Methods Here we use 38 hydroclimatic and slope predictors to project daily susceptibility under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 through 2100. CatBoost and XGBoost scores are averaged to provide a common basis for scenario comparisons. Results Maximum antecedent daily precipitation is the leading predictor in both models. Under SSP5-8.5, the annual fraction of grid cells classified as High or Very High increases by 4.37 percentage points per decade and reaches 51.2% in 2100. Increased susceptibility in June and September accompanies the July–August peak. For 2081–2100, the regional mean increases from 0.3103 to 0.3198 across precipitation perturbations of 0–50%, with progressively larger increments between successive levels. Discussion These results identify spatially heterogeneous hydroclimatic responses and a nonlinear regional-mean perturbation response, informing spatial and seasonal priorities for landslide monitoring.

papers.title: SweSolver: A Taichi-based GPU-accelerated 2D shallow water solver for large-scale surface flows
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: SweSolver is a Taichi-based GPU-accelerated two-dimensional shallow-water solver for large-scale surface flows over raster topography, including floods, landslides, and debris flows. Its applications include landslide-dam-break floods, flash-flood propagation, and landslide and debris-flow runout. The solver employs finite-volume MUSCL reconstruction and an HLLC-style Riemann solver on a Taichi sparse grid. It supports optional lateral-stress effects, volume-source inflow driven by a tabulated discharge hydrograph, and Manning, Coulomb, and Voellmy friction laws. This Zenodo record contains the source code, README, and example configuration. The input rasters and discharge hydrograph used in the associated paper are not included. If you use this code, please cite this Zenodo record.

ENGINEERING MONITORING OF DEFORMATIONS IN GEOSYNTHETIC-REINFORCED SOIL RETAINING STRUCTURES UNDER COMPLEX GEOLOGICAL CONDITIONS
papers.summary: The paper examines the applicability of geosynthetic-reinforced soil retaining structures for strengthening and restoring landslide-prone slopes under complex engineering-geological conditions. The causes of landslide processes, structural and technological solutions, and factors affecting the stability of reinforced soil structures are analyzed. Particular attention is paid to engineering and deformation monitoring, including the assessment of settlements and horizontal displacements as key indicators of serviceability and reliability. The performance of implemented structural solutions is evaluated, and the main parameters requiring monitoring are identified. The results substantiate the applicability of geosynthetic-reinforced soil structures for slope stabilization, restoration of damaged areas, and rehabilitation of engineering infrastructure.

papers.title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
papers.summary: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

papers.title: Immediate post-landslide mapping of critical road infrastructure using UAV surveys
papers.summary: Landslides pose a significant threat to transportation infrastructure, often causing sudden disruptions to national road networks that require rapid assessment to support emergency response and recovery planning. This study focuses on the immediate mapping of the Sykoula landslide in Aetolia-Acarnania, which significantly impacted a segment of the national road network using Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) surveys and GNSS measurements. The objective is to demonstrate the effectiveness of UAV-based photogrammetry for rapid, high-resolution data acquisition and analysis under time-sensitive conditions. The landslide occurred near the Sykoula settlement, approximately at the 127 km mark of the Ionian Highway, on the boundary between Arta and Aetolia-Acarnania. The landslide occurred within a mountainous corridor with known geohazard susceptibility, triggered by prolonged intense rainfall that saturated a sedimentary succession, reducing slope stability. As a result, a large volume of rock mass moved downslope, reaching the roadway and affecting both lanes, while a 200-meter-long ground rupture was reported along the highway alignment. In this framework, UAV surveys were deployed shortly after the event to capture high-resolution imagery over the area of interest. The dataset was processed using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) photogrammetry to generate detailed orthophotos, digital surface models (DSMs) and point clouds. UAV-based products assist in the precise delineation of landslide boundaries, the characterization of displacement patterns, the evaluation of landslide evolution, and the assessment of damage to the roadway and adjacent slopes. The results demonstrate that UAV-based mapping provides timely, high-resolution spatial information that can significantly enhance landslide response and infrastructure risk assessment.

papers.title: A multi-sensor framework for infrastructure resilience: integrating satellite EO and terrestrial surveys within the LAB_SAT project
papers.summary: The management of civil infrastructure and natural assets is a critical challenge for local authorities, necessitating robust, reliable monitoring strategies for hydrogeological and structural risk mitigation. To help close the gap between advanced remote‑sensing capabilities and municipal decision‑making, this work introduces the framework of the LAB_SAT Project (Agreement No. 2025‑9‑HB.0), a pilot initiative funded by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) under the Innovation for Downstream Preparation for Public Administrations (I4DP_PA) programme. The project seeks to establish an operational laboratory for assessing environmental hazards and monitoring infrastructure health. A multi-sensor approach is implemented, integrating Earth Observation (EO) data, leveraging SAR from COSMO-SkyMed and multispectral/hyperspectral imagery from Sentinel-2 and PRISMA, with terrestrial surveys, including UAV-based photogrammetry, GNSS, and Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS). Through the application of data-fusion algorithms and advanced scaling techniques, the system produces georeferenced indicators, fully interoperable with GIS environments, to support urban planning. These indicators are utilized to assess the stability of strategic assets, such as viaducts and historical buildings, and to monitor the impact of natural hazards like landslides and soil degradation. Key outputs include a Web-GIS digital platform and a prototype Digital Twin. By demonstrating the operational efficacy of satellite-derived information, the LAB_SAT project provides an integrated, replicable decision-support model for small municipalities. It enhances institutional capacity for evidence-based governance, promoting the synergy of remote sensing and non-destructive testing for the sustainable management of built and natural environments.

papers.title: Effect of Geotechnical Properties on Rainfall-Induced Landslide Probability: Infinite Slope Analysis and a Mechanics-Verified Hybrid Deep Learning Surrogate
papers.summary: Abstract Slopes are still judged on a single factor of safety (FoS), although two slopes with the same FoS can owe their strength to very different mixes of cohesion and friction. This study examines how much that matters in rain. Antecedent rain and a 24-h storm were routed into the slope with a slope-corrected Green–Ampt model; where the water perched above a less permeable layer, its pore pressure was applied slice by slice in a full-search Bishop analysis and on a planar slide along the layer. A physics-guided hybrid deep-learning surrogate (Hybrid-6), fitted to 21,000 Bishop solutions, made 3.3 × 10⁷ stability evaluations practical after its sensitivities and failure probabilities were checked against direct Bishop runs. For nine slopes of identical dry FoS (1.50), a 300-mm storm after 300 mm of antecedent rain increased the failure probability of friction-rich slopes 4.3–4.6 times more than that of cohesion-rich slopes (bootstrap 95% intervals within 4.0–5.0), and every rain-induced failure was translational. Applying the same water as a uniform pore-pressure ratio on the critical circle blurred this difference and reversed it at two of three slope angles. Within the conditions analysed, the planar FoS of the saturated layer described the storm-induced increase in failure probability (R² = 0.90, 54 cases), though less well for a withheld layer depth (Q² = 0.57). For the Rangamati (Bangladesh) landslides of 13 June 2017, the model limited the vulnerable slip depth to 1.4–2.1 m, and its predicted failure window contained the reported time of failure.

papers.title: Lifelines on the Edge: Understanding the Multiple-Hazard Risk to Critical Infrastructure at the Global Scale
papers.summary: Modern societies and economies depend on critical infrastructure (CI) to provide essential services, including electricity, telecommunications and water. Natural hazards can damage these assets, disrupt services and trigger cascading socioeconomic impacts far beyond the affected area. Recent disasters, including the 2021 floods in northwestern Europe and the 2024 Valencia floods, highlight the vulnerability of these lifelines. The aim of this thesis is to improve our understanding of global CI risk to multiple natural hazards by developing new datasets, exploring its vulnerability, and quantifying exposure and risk under present and future conditions. Chapter 2 develops a harmonized, spatially-explicit global CI dataset, including the Critical Infrastructure Spatial Index (CISI). Using OpenStreetMap (OSM), assets are mapped across seven sectors. The CISI measures infrastructure density on a scale from 0 to 1. Comparisons with population and gross domestic product (GDP) reveal strong global correlations, but considerable regional differences, with the strongest relationships in North America and Europe and the weakest in Africa. Chapter 3 addresses the fragmented evidence on infrastructure vulnerability to natural hazards. Through a systematic literature review, I synthesize existing fragility and vulnerability curves, which describe the probability and extent of damage at different hazard intensities. I compile an open-access, standardized database containing more than 1,510 curves for CI exposed to flooding, earthquakes, windstorms and landslides. A cross-hazard and cross-sector comparison also identifies important research gaps. Chapter 4 presents a probabilistic global assessment of CI risk from earthquakes, flooding, tropical cyclones and landslides. I estimate global expected annual damage (EAD) at USD 206 billion (range: USD 121–278 billion). Flooding contributes the largest share of EAD (56.4%), followed by earthquakes (21.4%) and rainfall-triggered landslide

papers.title: Effective operating procedures for advanced aerosol instruments at high-altitude observatories: A technical note
papers.summary: Advanced aerosol measurements at high-altitude observatories are scientifically valuable but operationally demanding, and the established standard procedures, such as those of WMO/GAW and ACTRIS, were developed largely for near sea level stations. This technical note sets out operating procedures for advanced aerosol instruments at high-altitude sites, with an emphasis on tropical observatories, and is intended to complement rather than restate those guidelines. Its organizing theme is the reduced ambient pressure that defines such sites: at 1600 m the pressure is about 840 hPa, roughly 17% below the sea level value. We describe how this single factor lowers pump suction and volumetric sample flow, increases the gas mean free path and hence the slip correction, the particle diffusion coefficient and ultrafine particle losses, and alters the internal operation of condensation particle counters, mobility spectrometers, aerodynamic and optical sizers, cloud condensation nuclei counters, aerosol mass spectrometers, and absorption photometers. We then treat the sampling system from inlet to instrument, including size cut off, whole air and interstitial inlets for in cloud and fog conditions, sample drying below 40% relative humidity, leak testing, and active flow control, followed by correction of the measured concentrations to standard temperature and pressure. Site selection, infrastructure, and meteorological instrumentation suited to harsh mountain conditions are also addressed. Procedures are illustrated for the NABHA Laboratory at Munnar, India. Residual instrument specific uncertainties at reduced pressure are identified as a direction for future work.

papers.title: Resilience to Landslides in the Lower Shullcas River Basin under Climate Change
papers.summary: The lower Shullcas River basin has a medium-high to low level of risk from landslides. This risk is made worse by geological, climatic, and topographic factors. Climate change, especially through intense rainfall and higher temperatures, increases this risk and makes it necessary to use proper mitigation strategies and more efficient urban development plans. Even so, there are still weaknesses in how risk management is integrated among the people and institutions involved in the territory. The purpose of this research was to identify the areas with the highest risk through mapping, and also to measure the resilience of the population exposed to the highest level of risk, in order to understand how they might respond and act during a possible disaster. For this purpose, methodologies based on risk prevention systems were used, aligned with SIGRID, CENEPRED, and INGEMMET. The results show favorable findings in some respects, since the study area, which includes the districts of Huancayo and El Tambo, presents medium-to-low landslide risk levels, with slopes ranging from 2% to 8%. The most critical zones are located along the marginal strip of the Shullcas River, where slopes reach up to 90% and where conditioning factors such as rainfall, river undercutting, and geomorphology turn these areas into constant hazards. The resilience evaluation shows less encouraging results, since most of the 50 residents surveyed near the highest-risk zone showed low levels of resilience compared with the coastal population of the country. Finally, it is recommended that more studies be carried out on different types of risk, including other triggering factors such as earthquakes, informal human activity, and geological aspects. It is also recommended to study wider areas because of the rapid population growth.

papers.title: Delay of flood formation by sponge-like porous bodies on unsaturated soil: a Richards' equation model
papers.summary: Sponge-like porous bodies (SPBs) offer a potential distributed storage approach for stormwater management in urban areas where space for conventional drainage solutions is limited. This paper builds upon our earlier up-flow SPB models, which are governed by mass conservation and Darcy's law. In contrast to earlier studies, infiltration into unsaturated soil with a water table at the bottom is described by the Richards equation. The soil is modeled with the Brooks–Corey relations, which is the reference model, and the problem is solved numerically. In addition, Gardner's conductivity model linearizes the Richards equation. This gives an analytical solution without the SPB and a semi-analytical solution with the SPB, and it allows the averaging over the soil surface that reduces the problem to one-dimensional. The analysis distinguishes two phases: absorption by the soil alone, and joint absorption by the soil and the SPB until ponding. The performance of the SPB is evaluated by comparing the flood formation times with and without the SPB, expressed as the efficiency, i.e., the relative delay of the flood formation. The results show that the SPB delays flood formation, and that the delay increases with the surface ratio and with the magnitude of the capillary head of the SPB.

papers.title: Experimental study on the shear strength and disintegration resistance of MICP-treated granite residual soil
papers.summary: To clarify the mechanisms by which microbial-induced calcite precipitation (MICP) stabilizes granite residual soil, this study investigates how clay content and treatment protocol affect its mechanical behavior and water stability. Soil samples formulated with distinct clay fractions were subjected to diverse MICP protocols and subsequently assessed through direct shear tests, disintegration experiments, and microscopic characterizations. The experimental outcomes indicate that bio-cementation effectively upgrades the overall structural integrity and hydro-durability of the matrices. Quantitatively, the biomineralization process yielded a dramatic 96.19% amplification in cohesion, alongside a 7.7% increment in the internal friction angle. Moreover, the evolution of shearing resistance displays a non-monotonic relationship with the clay fraction; as the fine-particle proportion increases, the shear strength initially diminishes—reaching a minimum at a 20% clay level—before escalating to its peak at a 40% clay content. In terms of disintegration resistance, while raw control specimens suffered total structural collapse within merely one minute of water immersion, the soils stabilized via a hybrid mixing and grouting MICP approach exhibited exceptional resilience with zero disintegration. Microscopic observations confirm that this integrated bio-treatment stimulates abundant calcium carbonate precipitation. These biogenic crystals fundamentally drive the macroscopic physical upgrades by occupying interstitial voids and firmly bridging adjacent soil aggregates. Moreover, the LFNMR (Low Field Nuclear Magnetic Resonance) test results demonstrate that MICP intervention efficiently diminishes the volume of both micro and total pores, promoting the understanding of MICP solidification mechanism from the calcium carbonate cementation at the macroscale to the pore structure at the microscale.

papers.summary: Landslides in the red beds are associated with potential slipping along structural planes, which is further aggravated by the presence of weak interlayers within these planes. These weak interlayers, characterized by soft red bed materials with loose structures, play a critical role in the slope slide. However, the precursors to sliding caused by these weak interlayers remain unclear. To address this, the study employed acoustic emission (AE) monitoring—an approach widely recognized for its effectiveness in detecting precursory signals—to investigate potential indicators of slip. AE monitoring was conducted during direct shear tests on red bed interlayers containing soft red rock layers to analyze their behavior prior to slip. The findings reveal that during shearing, the soft red bed in the interlayer first consolidates and then transitions into frictional sliding, resulting in complex and diverse stick-slip events. AE signals show a marked increase in AE activity preceding stick-slip events. Additionally, the friction coefficient increase during shearing is correlated with a decrease in the AE b -value. Furthermore, direct shear tests were conducted on red bed interlayers with varying water contents (10%, 20%, and 30%) to examine the influence of moisture on shear behavior. papers.title: The 2023 Emilia-Romagna Geo-Hydrological Disaster: Critical Decision-Making Issues Identified by Literature Review
papers.summary: In May 2023, the Emilia-Romagna region (northern Italy) was hit by two unexpected extreme weather events that caused 17 deaths, the displacing of 50,000 people, and damages amounting to over 10 billion euros. Such a geo-hydrological disaster has stimulated scientific investigation, and tens of papers have been published. In this systematic review, peer-reviewed publications are examined with the aim of identifying critical issues relevant to the decision-making process. These questions are crucial for policy-makers and territorial government agencies, who play a direct and fundamental role in disaster management. The review was performed in accordance with the PRISMA method and by the citation and indexing databases of Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). Its main findings are summarized as follows: (1) in flood and landslide mitigation, land-use planning adequate to the climate-adjusted scenarios must be designed and implemented; (2) early warning systems should be people-centered and based on more advanced weather forecasts or new methods, like the elaboration of cellular geo-referenced data; (3) the use of integrated approaches based on machine learning and other modern technologies is increasingly being proposed to improve performance in disaster response. It is apparent that the reviewed literature can inform policy for improving government guidelines, rules, and decision-making in disaster management.

papers.title: MONITORING AND ASSESSMENT OF SURFACE WATER QUALITY IN THE THA THONG RIVER INFLUENCED BY DOLOMITE MINING ACTIVITIES, SURATTHANI PROVINCE, THAILAND
papers.summary: Maintaining surface water quality within regulatory standards is important local communities and ecosystems. The present study aims to monitor and assess the surface water quality in the Thathong River, Surat Thani Province, specifically within the dolomite mining zone throughout the rainy season (May - July 2025). Water samples were taken from 9 monitoring stations to determine physicochemical parameters and amounts of heavy metal. Water temperatures varied from 30.3 to 33.1 °C, electrical conductivity (EC) from 345 to 406 µS/cm, total dissolved solids (TDS) from 173 to 202 mg/L, and total suspended solids (SS) from 1.01 to 34.01 mg/L, with a TDS/EC ratio of 0.50. The value of pH ranged from 7.9 to 8.6, dissolved oxygen (DO) from 9 to 12 mg/L, and biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) from 0.02 to 2 mg/L. The average mean of nitrate-nitrogen and orthophosphate was 2.14 ± 0.84 mg/L and 0.20 ± 0.01 mg/L, respectively. Low quantities of copper, iron, manganese, and lead were discovered, while cadmium and arsenic were not detectable. All detected heavy metals were below the Thailand’s class 3 surface water quality standard. The findings provide baseline information to support long-term monitoring and water resource management in mining - influenced catchments. According to spatial analysis, land-use activities and soil erosion within mining sites was associated with nutrient accumulation and water - quality deterioration. These results provide essential baseline information for managing water resources and for planning policies and regulations to support long-term environmental monitoring and preservation.

papers.title: Seamounts: le montagne sottomarine del Mediterraneo, hotspots di biodiversità
papers.summary: Within the PNRR MER Project, 79 Italian seamounts (200–3000 m) were surveyed using MBES, SBP and ROV Work Class (WROV). This large-scale national assessment updated seafloor geomorphology, revealing previouslyunidentified features like pockmarks and landslides. Integrated ROV video analysis allowed for detailed geological, biological and habitat characterization, identifying key benthic components, and their conservation status. This dataset provides a robust baseline to assess vulnerability and guide restoration strategies, supporting the goal of protecting 30% of Italian seas by 2030.

From participation to data: collaborative mapping in the context of natural hazards and risks
papers.summary: Collaborative mapping has emerged as a key approach for collecting, analysing, and sharing geospatial information on natural hazards and risks. By integrating Citizen Science (CS) and Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI), it incorporates local knowledge, real-time observations, and crowdsourced data collection into risk assessment and management processes, where traditional data sources are limited or outdated. This study provides a systematic overview of collaborative mapping applications for natural hazards, including hydrogeomorphological (floods, landslides, coastal erosion), climate and weather related (storms and cyclones, wildfires, droughts and heat waves) and geophysical (earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions) as well as multi-hazards contexts, examining how different terminologies, actor types, and technological approaches are represented across the literature. A total of 105 peer-reviewed studies were selected following a screening process based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, starting from major scientific databases. The results highlight an uneven distribution of research efforts, with a focus on floods and multi-hazard contexts. Furthermore, collaborative mapping is predominantly applied in mitigation, preparedness, and response phases. In terms of technologies, while traditional GIS-based methods dominate, computational approaches like Machine Learning (ML) are gaining traction. These approaches increasingly rely on the combined use of complementary geospatial sources: satellite and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery commonly serves as a basemap guiding the digitisation of features in OpenStreetMap (OSM), whose data are then extracted and integrated into hazard and risk analyses. This integration enables spatial datasets to be rapidly created and updated where authoritative data are scarce or outdated, thereby supporting disaster management across its different phases. papers.title: Assessment of IMD-HRRR Model in Predicting Extreme Rainfall Events over India
papers.summary: Abstract Climate vulnerability in India has intensified due to the increasing frequency of hydro-meteorological extreme rainfall events (EREs). While numerical weather prediction (NWP) models have improved for large-scale medium-range forecasting, precipitation forecasting, especially for extreme events, remains less reliable due to simplified representations of topography, land cover, and vegetation in global models. To address this, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) operates the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (IMD-HRRR) model at 2 km horizontal resolution, assimilating hourly radar and surface observations to provide 12-hour nowcasts updated every 2 hours. This study evaluates the performance of the IMD-HRRR model in predicting extremely heavy rainfall events (≥ 204.4 mm/day) across mainland India in 2023. The IMD gauge-adjusted merged rainfall product GSMaP_ISRO (0.1° × 0.1°, hourly) was utilised to compare model forecasts using traditional metrics (bias, RMSE, correlation, and critical success index) and the Extreme Dependency Score (EDS), which is better suited for rare events. Results indicate that IMD-HRRR generally captures the spatial distribution of extreme rainfall over the Northwest, Northeast, and South Peninsular domains, with peak activity correctly predicted over Meghalaya, Assam, and the Western Ghats. However, systematic dry biases were observed across all domains (-0.61 to -0.93 mm/12 h), with higher root mean square deviation in the Northwest (~ 1.79 mm) and Northeast/South Peninsular regions (~ 3.54 mm). The model exhibits a slight dry bias over the Western Himalayas and Kutch, a wet bias over the Western Ghats, and an accurate representation of the Konkan–Karnataka coastal rainfall belt. EDS analysis confirms the model's ability to capture extreme events. papers.title: Geomorphological Characteristics Based on RS and GIS Analysis and Land Use/Land Cover Dynamics in Anambra State, Southeastern Nigeria

papers.summary: The geological and geomorphological characteristics of a region significantly influence its land use patterns and environmental management strategies. This study aims to analyze the slope distribution and its implications on LULC in a part of Anambra State, providing insights into the region's suitability for various land uses and potential risks. Steeper slopes (7.94 - 28.51 degrees) cover a minimal area of 9.42 km². papers.summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.0) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. papers.title: An Integrated Methodological Framework with Historical Validation for Flood and Debris-Flow Hazard Zoning in Ungauged Andean Catchments
papers.summary: Flash floods and debris flows in Andean–Amazonian mountain catchments rank among the most destructive natural hazards, and the headwater catchments where they originate almost invariably lack hydrometric records, placing them within the classical problem of Predictions in Ungauged Basins (PUB). Hazard maps generated for these environments from open data share a critical weakness: they are released without empirical validation against observed events, so their credibility rests on unverified assumptions. This study proposes OF-VAL (Open-data Flood Hazard Framework with Historical VALidation), a six-stage framework based entirely on open-access data whose distinguishing feature is a validation gate: hazard products are released only if the model, forced with an open-data reconstruction of a documented historical event, reproduces the observed impact footprint above a predefined threshold (F≥0.50). The framework is demonstrated in the ungauged Sicre–Ipal microcatchment (Cusco, Peru; 19.41 km2), using as benchmark the debris flow of 21 December 2018 documented by INGEMMET and delineated on 0.7 m PeruSAT-1 imagery. A process-class compatibility rule (R1.4) screens the benchmark before gate execution: the event’s documented genesis as a landslide-dam outburst, together with four concordant open-data estimates of the event rainfall (6.3 and 9.7 mm day−1 at the two governing SENAMHI stations, 7.5 mm at the PISCOpd cell and 18.2 mm in GPM IMERG, all an order of magnitude below debris-flow triggering thresholds), establishes that the flow was not pluvially generated; the reconstruction executed with the largest of these estimates wets at most 5.6 ha against a 15.5 ha deposit, so the fit index is bounded at F≤0.36 and gate G4a is declared not executable with this benchmark. papers.title: Geological Characterization and Soil Erodibility Factors in Parts of Southeastern, Nigeria
papers.source: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHY AND ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT
papers.summary: This study focuses on analyzing soil erodibility in five Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Imo State, Nigeria: Isu, Mbaitoli, Njaba, Orlu, and Oru East. These areas are prone to flooding due to their location within the lower Niger River Basin, exacerbating soil erosion. The study aims to evaluate geological and soil characteristics influencing landslide susceptibility in these LGAs. The aim of this study is to assess soil erodibility factors and geological characteristics in Imo State, Nigeria, focusing on Isu, Mbaitoli, Njaba, Orlu, and Oru East LGAs. It involves identifying predominant soil types, calculating Soil Erodibility Factor (K), and mapping erosion susceptibilities. The study correlates data with hydrological and climatic information to analyze landslide risks and propose mitigation strategies. This study utilizes data primarily from the Soil Map of the World, version 3.6, corrected for errors and updated for relevance. Geographic Information System (GIS) tools are employed for spatial analyses, including mapping soil types and erosion susceptibilities. The study also integrates topographical data to understand elevation variations and geological formations impacting soil characteristics. The study identifies two primary soil types: Dystric Nitosols covering 578.63 km² and Xanthic Ferralsols covering 0.064 km². Dystric Nitosols have a low Soil Erodibility Factor (K) of 0.017769 t.ha.h.ha/MJ/mm, indicating good structural stability and less susceptibility to erosion. In contrast, Xanthic Ferralsols exhibit a higher K-factor of 0.018724 t.ha.h.ha/MJ/mm, suggesting greater vulnerability to erosion due to their acidic nature and lower fertility. The spatial distribution of soil types and their erodibility factors highlights significant implications for agricultural productivity and environmental conservation. papers.title: Google Earth Engine–Based Landslide Early Warning System (GLEWS) for Rainfall-Induced Landslides in Idukki, India
papers.summary: We have developed a Google Earth Engine–based landslide early warning system, named GLEWS, designed to issue landslide alerts for Idukki. The GLEWS uses 3-hour global precipitation measurement (GPM) integrated multi-satellite retrievals for GPM precipitation data and hourly global forecast system rainfall forecasts in combination with a slope stability factor of safety (FoS) map at 30 m resolution, where FoS ≤ 1.5 indicates high susceptibility and FoS > 2.0 indicates stability. The system integrates live rainfall telemetry from eight automatic weather stations to calibrate satellite precipitation using conditional merging, combining an inverse distance weighting–interpolated error field with gauge observations. A critical daily rainfall of 213 mm and a critical antecedent rainfall of 2,921 mm separate extreme from non-extreme precipitation. Alerts are issued as red (extremely critical), orange (very critical), yellow (critical), and green (not critical) based on rainfall exceedance and slope FoS. In the August 15, 2018, case study, GLEWS achieved 72.6 percent sensitivity with conditional merging using five India Meteorological Department (IMD) point-gauge observations with partial gauge correction, compared with 8.9 percent using uncalibrated or IMD 0.25° gridded precipitation, demonstrating that point-level gauge observations are essential for operational performance. A second case study using the July 7, 2023, Munnar Gap Road landslide showed that conditional merging increased the daily rainfall estimate from 20.0 mm (raw GPM) to 63.9 mm, a threefold improvement. The system has been ported from JavaScript to Python enabling automated gauge ingestion and autonomous operation during monsoon seasons.

papers.title: Fissure-controlled preferential infiltration and hydro-mechanical response of a red-bed landslide under contrasting rainfall patterns
papers.summary: Introduction Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most common and destructive geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions. Rainfall infiltration modifies the hydraulic state and effective stress of slope materials, thereby contributing to slope instability. Fissures can provide preferential infiltration pathways, but the hydro-mechanical responses of fissure-developed landslides under different rainfall patterns remain insufficiently understood. Methods This study investigates the Wangjiangao red-bed landslide in Jishou City, Hunan Province, China. A two-dimensional coupled saturated-unsaturated seepage-stress model was subsequently established in FLAC3D. The displacement-calibrated simulations reproduced the general deformation trends and indicated that the degree of saturation at a deep observation point within an equivalent high-permeability zone increased from approximately 45% to nearly 99% during intense rainfall. papers.title: Geological and climatic controls on landslide susceptibility and hazard along the Amarnath pilgrimage corridor, Kashmir Himalaya
papers.summary: Landslides are a recurrent and increasingly consequential hazard across the Himalaya, where steep terrain, tectonically weakened lithologies, climatic variability, and expanding anthropogenic activity interact to destabilize slopes. This study assesses landslide susceptibility along the Baltal-Amarnath-Panjtarni-Poshpathri pilgrimage corridor in the upper Sind catchment, Jhelum basin of the Kashmir Himalaya, India, using an integrated framework that combines high-resolution remote sensing, field-based geological mapping, geotechnical investigations, and climate-data analysis. We developed a meso-scale landslide susceptibility model at 1:10,000 m using 18 conditioning factors and evaluated against field-verified landslide events. The model achieved AUC values of 0.80 for the success-rate (training) curve and 0.86 for the prediction-rate (validation) curve, indicating good model fit and predictive capability, respectively. About 16% is classified as highly susceptible and 68.1% as moderately susceptible to slope failures along the corridor. Landslides are concentrated primarily on steep, structurally deformed lithological formations, debris-mantled slopes modified by road cuts, and active drainage lines. Structural and kinematic analyses indicate that slope instability is strongly influenced by discontinuities and weak lithological units associated with the Main Central Thrust zone in the area. Climate analysis indicates a warming trend of nearly 2 °C in recent decades, substantial interannual variability in snow cover, and an increasing influence of extreme precipitation events, including cloudbursts and intense monsoonal rainfall. papers.title: A Numerical Study on Road Embankment Stability Enhanced by Natural Reinforcement
papers.source: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology
papers.summary: This study numerically evaluates the effect of natural reinforcements on the stabilization of a road embankment built with poorly graded granular soil (SP - SM). The response of the structure under a continuous vehicular surcharge load of 24 kN/m² is analyzed using the GeoStudio suite, with the SLOPE/W and SIGMA/W programs utilized for limit equilibrium stability and finite element stress-deformation analyses, respectively. The unreinforced soil embankment yields a Factor of Safety (FOS) of 1.133, which falls below the Indian Roads Congress (IRC) accepted level of stability. Banana Fiber Geotextiles (BFG) are applied as planar reinforcement at varying vertical spacings from 0.25 m to 1.50 m. It is found that the optimum techno-economic spacing of 1.0 m results in a 36.6 % increase in FOS and a 46.4 % reduction in peak internal shear strain. In parallel, the bio-reinforced model, simulating a 2.0 m deep 6-month-old vetiver grass root matrix at the slope face, achieves an FOS of 1.406. Finite element contours reveal that the bio-reinforced zone, modeled as an equivalent-continuum block, provides significant structural confinement. The biological confinement completely arrests lateral face yielding, decreasing horizontal displacement by 70.8 %, reducing maximum vertical settlement by 60.0 %, and dropping peak internal shear strain by 80.0 %. Both natural reinforcement methods successfully satisfy the safety thresholds recommended by IRC: 75-2015, proving that bio-reinforcement provides superior deformation control and establishes itself as a highly effective, sustainable alternative to conventional stabilization techniques.

papers.title: ALLO: Adaptive Landslide Learning Observatory
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: ALLO is a research prototype of an early-warning and decision-support system for rainfall-triggered landslides on Andean hillslopes, with Manizales (Caldas, Colombia) as its initial case. A TypeScript agentic bot orchestrates weather ingestion, a Python (FastAPI) stochastic simulation service with an in-process TypeScript failover engine, and a language-model layer that explains results but does not compute them. The scientific core models latent soil saturation as a rainfall-forced bounded Jacobi (Wright-Fisher) diffusion with an exponential hazard link, propagated by seeded Monte Carlo and mapped to four alert levels anchored to the 25-day antecedent-rainfall index (A25) of the Manizales early-warning system. The repository includes the project model card and an executable regression suite that carries the model card's invariants into the user-facing explanation layer.

papers.title: UAV-Enabled Installation of Wireless Sensors for Monitoring Inaccessible Cliffs and/or Emergencies
papers.summary: Monitoring is frequently used to study landslides (instabilities in soil and rock slopes) and to manage the risk when a focused mechanism is underway. To date, most of the so-called ‘geotechnical sensors’ and some surveying systems must be installed manually on the landslide body. In some scenarios this installation phase may imply a high risk for operators. To overcome these issues, we developed a simple system to install wireless sensors by means of Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV), which is presented in the paper along with the tests carried out. Concretely, we deployed several wireless precision tiltmeters able to acquire and transmit attitude readings using LOng-RAnge communication capability. The experiments were conducted in an area of paramount geomechanical and societal interest: the Montserrat massif (Barcelona, Spain), threatened by medium-to-large rockfalls. The procedure to attach the sensor to the UAV, release it, and glue it to the ground is described. Some of the results and issues that emerged are also presented and discussed. The tests show that the installation of sensors with UAVs can complement the monitoring techniques already available in the aforementioned special situations. The UAV-enabled deployment method should be considered as a means to speed up the availability of real-time data to monitor critical, hazardous situations.

papers.title: Landslide-generated tsunamis at Stromboli Volcano (Italy): characterization, detection, and modelling using broadband seismometers and sea-level records for early warning purposes
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Volcanic landslides recurrently occur along the Sciara del Fuoco (SdF), the NW flank of Stromboli (Aeolian Archipelago, SE Tyrrhenian Sea), frequently entering the sea and triggering near-field tsunamis, a significant secondary hazard for coastal communities. Volcanic activity is monitored through a multi-sensor network, including two offshore and one coastal sea-level gauge, the instrumental basis of the tsunami early warning system. Integrating broadband seismometers could further improve early warning capabilities. This thesis investigates the detection and characterization of tsunami signatures in seismic records, demonstrating the feasibility of coastal broadband seismometers for real-time, automatic tsunami detection and integration into the early warning framework. Six modest-volume tsunamigenic landslides occurring between 2019 and 2024, producing local tsunamis with wave heights ≤ 2 m, were analyzed as test cases. Coastal records reveal clear tsunami signatures as very-long-period (VLP) oscillations, most evident on horizontal components, peaking at 0.005–0.02 Hz with periods of 70–120 s. A template-matching algorithm proved highly effective for automatic real-time landslide detection, outperforming the conventional STA/LTA method. The tsunami-related VLP signals are interpreted as ground tilt induced by quasi-static tsunami loading. Focusing on the 3 July 2019 event, we modeled this elastic deformation using tsunami propagation outputs, achieving a satisfactory fit with observed tilt signals and capturing the early tsunami phase. Clear tilt signals emerged 0.6–1.5 minutes before tsunami arrival at nearby gauges, demonstrating short-term early-warning potential. Tilt amplitudes (0.02–0.17 µrad) decreased with distance from the coast, remaining detectable up to ~500 m, underscoring the importance of station proximity. papers.title: Predicting Natural Disasters Using Artificial Intelligence And Machine Learning: A Review Of Methods, Data Sources And Early Warning Architectures
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Floods, earthquakes, cyclones, landslides and droughts cause heavy loss of life and property, and their impact depends strongly on how early communities are warned. Conventional physics-based forecasting remains essential, but it struggles to exploit the volume and variety of data now produced by satellites, ground sensors and historical archives. This paper reviews how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are being used to estimate disaster risk and support early warning. It surveys data sources, including rainfall, river levels, seismic waveforms, reanalysis fields and satellite imagery, and examines models ranging from random forests and support vector machines for susceptibility mapping to long short-term memory networks for flood forecasting, convolutional and transformer networks for earthquake detection, and graph-based models for medium-range weather prediction. A five-layer architecture for an AI-assisted early warning system is proposed, linking data ingestion, preprocessing, hazard-specific models, risk fusion and alert dissemination. The paper identifies research gaps such as data scarcity in ungauged regions, limited uncertainty reporting and the weak connection between forecasts and community action. It concludes that AI predictions should be treated as decision support that complements, rather than replaces, physical models and expert judgement.

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility mapping using deep learning in Dak Lak, Vietnam
papers.source: Journal of Science and Transport Technology
papers.summary: Landslides cause significant damage to transportation infrastructure, settlements, and agricultural land in the Central Highlands of Vietnam, particularly in the former Dak Lak province. Therefore, identifying areas with the potential for landslide occurrence is essential to support land-use planning and the development of landslide mitigation measures. This study proposes an explainable deep-learning framework for landslide susceptibility assessment using four models: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Deep Residual Dense Network (DRDN), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN). An inventory comprising 235 landslide polygons was analyzed together with 14 conditioning factors, including aspect, slope, curvature, elevation, geology, land use, soil type, rainfall, distance to faults, distance to roads, distance to rivers, the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), the topographic wetness index (TWI), and flow accumulation. The results showed that CNN achieved the best performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) = 0.913, a mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.197, and a root mean square error (RMSE) = 0.444 for the training dataset, and AUC = 0.888, MAE = 0.251, and RMSE = 0.501 for the validation dataset. Model interpretation showed that landslide susceptibility was notably influenced by slope, mean annual rainfall, geological factors, and distance to roads. The effects of these factors were nonlinear and varied across different value ranges, while their response patterns also differed among individual locations. A spatial accuracy assessment of the susceptibility map showed that the high and very high susceptibility classes occupied only 18.30% of the study area but contained 94.88% of the observed landslide pixels. In particular, the very high susceptibility class occupied 7.51% of the study area, contained 68.18% of the landslide pixels, and recorded the highest frequency ratio of 9.079. papers.title: Modern Approaches to Reducing Landslide Disaster Risk: Integrating Remote Sensing, Machine Learning, and Community Preparedness
papers.source: International Journal of Emerging Trends in Engineering and Development
authors: Dr. Rajesh Arora Dipendra Nath Subedi
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are major natural disasters that cause severe loss of life and massive economic damage worldwide. This paper reviews current strategies for reducing landslide disaster risk, focusing on three main areas: advanced susceptibility mapping, remote sensing technologies, and community-based disaster management. Using a systematic review approach, we analyze 15 recent scientific studies to understand how modern technology can be applied to real-world risk reduction. The findings show that artificial intelligence and remote sensing greatly improve the accuracy of early warning systems and hazard mapping. However, technology alone is not enough; community hazard knowledge and social preparedness are absolutely essential for saving lives. We conclude that a blended approach combining engineering technology with local community planning is the most effective way to reduce landslide disaster risks. Keywords: Landslide Risk Reduction; Remote Sensing; Machine Learning; Disaster Management; Early Warning Systems; Susceptibility Mapping; Community Preparedness.

papers.summary: Abstract. High-resolution convection-permitting models (CPMs) provide vital datasets for studying localized extreme precipitation and associated multi-hazard risks like landslides and floods. Yet validating CPM datasets against observations remains a challenge. This study evaluates two sub-daily CPM datasets, VHR-REA_IT and LAM-HIND, against observations over a 10-year period across two Italian regions: Emilia-Romagna and Campania. Extreme precipitation is defined using the 95th percentile of wet-event intensities across accumulation durations of 1, 2, 4, 12, and 24 hours. Conventional verification metrics only partially assess dataset performance and hide differences in the temporal organization of precipitation extremes. Observations show that STWEs and LTWEs are only partially associated. Depending on region and season, around 7–15 % of observed 1-hour STWEs are embedded within 24-hour LTWEs. papers.title: Integrated Geotechnical Properties and GIS-Based Analysis for Landslide Susceptibility Zonation in Aring 8, Gua Musang, Malaysia
papers.summary: Landslides threaten tropical mountainous regions where rainfall, weathering, and geological complexity destabilise slopes. This study assessed landslide susceptibility across 25 km2 of Aring 8, Gua Musang, Malaysia, using geotechnical testing and GIS-based multi-criteria mapping. Granite residual soils (GR1, GR2) and tuff residual soils (T1, T2) underwent geotechnical investigations, including moisture content, particle size distribution, Atterberg limits, and proctor tests. Tuff residual soil T2 recorded the highest moisture content (31.42 ± 4.45%) and a plasticity index of 12.41% (GR1 recorded the highest PI of 15.36%), along with 8% clay fraction and maximum dry density (MDD) of 1.75 g/cm3 at 17% optimum moisture content (OMC). Granitic residual soil, GR1 exhibited a particle-size distribution of 30% gravel, 48% sand, 19% silt, and 3% clay with an OMC of 20% and MDD of 1.55 g/cm3. Particle-size distributions indicated predominantly coarse-grained soils. Landslide Susceptibility Index (LSI = Σ w_i × r_i) incorporating elevation, slope gradient, aspect, soil series, and lithology, delineated low-, moderate-, and high-susceptibility zones. High susceptibility was associated with slopes exceeding 25°, structurally controlled drainage, unpaved logging roads, and high-plasticity clayey-silt mantles. These spatial associations suggest combined geological, hydrological, and anthropogenic influences on instability. This zonation supports preliminary land-use planning and slope mitigation.

papers.title: Non-eruptive debris flows at Mount Shasta: historical record, drivers, and implications for future hazards
papers.summary: Assessments of water-driven mass flows at snow and ice-covered volcanoes are often based on the assumption that the most impactful flows will happen during eruptions (lahars). However, as eruptions are a relatively low-probability event, non-eruptive debris flows tied to precipitation or glacial outburst floods may be more common. This is especially relevant at Mount Shasta, one of the southernmost glaciated stratovolcanoes in the Cascade volcanic arc, where past hazards assessments focused on the possibility of larger flows triggered by eruptive activity. Recent years (2021–2025) at Mount Shasta, however, have seen smaller non-eruptive lahars (locally called ‘debris flows’), which have had significant impacts on the communities and infrastructure surrounding the volcano, disrupting major transportation routes and threatening municipal water supplies. Given Mount Shasta’s current quiescence, it is prudent to focus volcanic hazard assessment on these non-eruptive lahars. In this study, we expand the historical record of debris flow occurrence and determine whether there is a discernible link between debris flow frequency and broader, meteorological forces. We classify debris flows into two broad groups based on associated meteorological parameters: (1) flows triggered by rainfall during storms, and (2) flows without associated precipitation occurring during hot summer days in years with widespread drought, including below average snow accumulation in the previous winter. These findings are consistent with historical anecdotal observations by local residents – that debris flow occurrence outside of precipitation is more frequent in hot, dry summers – and provide important information for evaluating which meteorological conditions may lead to an increase in debris flow occurrence. papers.title: Current state and features of landslide process development within the territory of Dnipro city and Dnipropetrovsk region
papers.source: Bridges and tunnels Theory Research Practice
papers.summary: Purpose of the research is to analyse the current state of landslide-prone territories in Dnipro city and Dnipropetrovsk region, identify the main natural and technogenic factors controlling the development and activation of landslide processes, and substantiate the necessity for further research into the stability of soil slopes within urbanised territories. Methodology. The research was carried out on the basis of a comprehensive analysis of literature sources, materials from the state monitoring of exogenous geological processes, engineering-geological, geomorphological, and hydrogeological materials, cartographic information, and statistical data on the development of landslide processes within the territory of Dnipro city and Dnipropetrovsk region. Methods of systematisation, comparative analysis, and data generalisation were applied to assess the current state of landslide-prone territories and identify the factors affecting slope stability. Findings. The current state of landslide process development in Dnipropetrovsk region and Dnipro city has been analysed, and the territories with the highest concentration of active and potentially hazardous landslides have been identified. It has been established that the activation of landslide processes is caused by the combined influence of natural factors, including geological structure, relief, hydrogeological conditions, erosion processes, and climatic factors, as well as technogenic impacts associated with urban development, disturbance of natural drainage conditions, leakage from engineering networks, and uncontrolled surface runoff. papers.summary: The 2000 Payatas landfill collapse in Quezon City, Philippines in which hundreds of people were crushed by an avalanche of trash after a landslide at a landfill created by illegal trash disposal was a critical destabilizing event that changed the solid waste governance regime for the Philippines. It led to the passing of Republic Act 9003 (Ecological Solid Waste Management Act). Twenty plus years have passed since this event and while there has been progress towards ecological solid waste management it is still incomplete. papers.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Advancing Hydropower Development in Nepal
papers.summary: This paper discusses and reviews the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) in the development of hydropower project in Nepal. Nepal has immense potential in hydropower and significant energy resources, which could strengthen the energy sector, increase GDP and support the sustainable economic growth. The use of AI in this field could drive innovation in hydropower and water resource management. AI can be applied to the study of river morphology, hydrology, sedimentation, debris flow, landslides and the risk of lake or dam outburst floods. Case from Nepal show that the emerging use of AI in hydropower. However, its wider adoption will improved data availability, better sensor networks, enhance technical capacity and stronger institutional support.

papers.title: EERI Virtual Earthquake Reconnaissance Team (VERT): Phase 1 Response to the M7.7 Pitaloza Arriba, Panama Earthquake, October 9, 2026, in EERI 2026 Pitaloza Arriba, Panama Earthquake Reconnaissance
papers.summary: This report describes reconnaissance findings which were conducted virtually as part of the Earthquake Engineering Research Institute's (EERI) Learning from Earthquakes (LFE) Virtual Earthquakes Reconnaissance Team (VERT). VERT is a team of volunteers that activate after major earthquakes to curate reports on the impact to the community. VERT activates in a series of phases after an earthquake to assist in-field teams with data-driven reconnaissance. This report is VERT's Phase 1 report for the M7.7 Pitaloza Arriba, Panama earthquake that occurred on October 9th, 2026. The report summarizes earthquake characteristics, aftershocks, and emergency response, as well as geotechnical hazards such as tsunami and landslide impacts. The report also summarizes the impacts to the region on a variety of different topics, including public health, schools, buildings, housing, transportation, and utilities. This report is based on publicly available data after the events. The assessment provided in the report is performed by the judgment of the authors with limited access to ground-truthing. Data in this report are intended to give a rapid overview of earthquake impacts and inform potential field reconnaissance efforts.

papers.title: Reply on RC1
papers.summary: Abstract. Rainfall-triggered landslides cause thousands of fatalities each year, yet effective early warning remains challenging across many mountainous regions because of sparse rainfall observations and limited forecasting infrastructure. Here we present ALERT (Automated Landslide Early Risk Tracker), a scalable, cloud-native framework that integrates NASA IMERG satellite precipitation, ECMWF operational forecasts, terrain susceptibility, rainfall intensity–duration thresholds, debris-flow runout modelling, and building exposure to deliver near-real-time, impact-based landslide warnings. ALERT incorporates a globally transferable catalogue of 24 rainfall thresholds while allowing user-defined thresholds and susceptibility layers, enabling deployment across diverse climatic and geomorphological settings. Event-based validation achieved a sensitivity of 0.80 and an overall accuracy exceeding 0.70, demonstrating effective detection of hazardous rainfall conditions for landslide initiation. By reducing dependence on dense ground-based rain-gauge networks, ALERT provides a computationally efficient and scalable pathway towards regional scale landslide early warning and climate-resilient disaster risk reduction, particularly in data-scarce regions.

papers.title: Editorial: Big data mining and artificial intelligence in earth science
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) for geoscience uses intelligent algorithms to extract concealed patterns from big Earth data, enabling more accurate predictions and decisions in scientific discoveries and applications, such as Earth's evolution, geological modeling, environmental monitoring, hazard mitigation, and resource exploration (Zhou et al., 2018(Zhou et al., , 2026)). Its evolution has followed a clear paradigm transition-from early expert systems through data-driven machine learning, to the current physics-informed, knowledge-data dual-driven approaches (Zhou et al., 2018;Zuo et al., 2023;Cheng et al., 2025). This progression is not merely incremental; it is fundamentally reshaping geoscience by integrating big data analytics with machine learning algorithms, and in doing so, redefining the practices of many researchers and engineers in their daily work (Zuo et al., 2023;Zhou et al., 2026). This is the reason why this special topic issue comes to exist here. It is devoted to showcase recent advances in the research and application of AI across many geoscience disciplines.
