papers.title: Worth waiting for, hardly worth waiting: data latency and the timing of regional landslide warnings in China
papers.summary: Abstract. Landslide warning services must weigh the better evidence that later data bring against the lead time lost while waiting for them. We studied this trade-off for 280 rainfall-induced landslides in China (2015–2024) with minute-, hour- or period-level occurrence times reported in the news, using the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission's Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) precipitation and as-issued Global Forecast System (GFS) forecasts in a latency-aware retrospective replay. In a case-crossover design, observed rainfall replacing forecasts added substantial information (matched area under the receiver operating characteristic curve +0.058 [0.034, 0.081]), whereas later satellite runs and newer forecast cycles added little or none. In a rolling replay of 24 h warnings, waiting one 6 h step before issuing gave no stable gain in detection at warning loads of 0.5–10 % of cell-time. In a cost–loss analysis, issuing at once with satellite rainfall plus forecast reached a relative economic value (REV, dimensionless) of 0.55, close to a latency-free benchmark (0.57) and above a rainfall threshold (0.34) and, on matched 2015–2020 decisions, the archived version 2.0.0 Landslide Hazard Assessment for Situational Awareness (LHASA) nowcast (0.34). A value-of-information waiting rule added +0.002 [−0.005, +0.007] over the best fixed policy, averaged across the exploratory cost–loss range. The pre-specified cost–loss test could not discriminate, because almost no rule warns at its cost–loss ratios, but a second test, fixed before an independent 2008–2014 sample was assembled, detected a value of waiting when no forecast was available (+0.03 [0.01, 0.05] in REV). Brackets give 95 % confidence intervals. With both satellite rainfall and forecasts available, waiting rarely repaid its lead-time cost.

papers.title: Activities of the Japan Disaster Charter for the 2026 Kumamoto Earthquake
papers.source: Journal of the Japan society of photogrammetry and remote sensing
papers.summary: The Japan Disaster Charter is an operational framework for the integrated use of public and commercial Earth-observation satellites during disasters. Following the M7.1 earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture on 28 July 2026, the Charter was activated three minutes after the event. Multiple SAR satellites, including StriX, QPS-SAR, and Capella, were tasked during the first night, followed by high-resolution optical observations by Pleiades Neo and Pleiades the next day. Satellite data were interpreted to identify landslides and building and infrastructure damage, and the resulting information products were delivered to disaster-management agencies as maps, GIS data, and PDF reports. This paper describes the observation strategy and operational workflow from satellite tasking to product delivery and discusses the significance of combining multiple satellite resources for rapid, wide-area damage assessment.

The hilly morphology, high rainfall, and residential activities increase the vulnerability of this area to disasters. The main challenges faced by the community are the limited scientific information regarding subsurface conditions and the low capacity of residents to understand the causes of landslides and science-based mitigation measures. papers.title: Sequential high-density radiocarbon dating to detect invisible event layers in marine sediments
papers.summary: Abstract We present a unique application of radiocarbon measurements on hemipelagic sediments that uses continuous radiocarbon dating of total organic carbon ( 14 C TOC age) to recognize event deposits. The 14 C TOC age of sediments is not commonly used for age determination because total organic carbon includes various origins, such as marine, terrestrial, and reworked old fragments. In this study, the 14 C TOC ages of some horizons were found to be older than those of the deeper ones through continuous 14 C TOC measurements at 0.5- to 1.0-cm intervals. The reversal 14 C TOC ages resulted not from the settlement of organic particles from the terrestrial environments, such as floodings, but from the submarine slope failures. Therefore, we can regard the reversal 14 C TOC layers as event layers due to geohazards. After reconstruction of the age model using foraminiferal tests obtained from the sediment core used in this study, depositional ages of event layers were identified. Well correlation with historical natural disasters after the 15 th century suggest validity of the method proposed by the current study.

papers.title: Reconstructing Landslide Erosion Volumes from Post-Event Topography
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Landslide volume controls hillslope sediment budgets, but measuring it requires a pre-event high-resolution digital terrain model (DTM), which is rarely available. We reconstruct the pre-event surface inside scars from a single post-event lidar DTM and scar outlines. Rim interpolation gives a first surface, and a gradient-boosted model restores the slope convexity that interpolation cannot represent. Trained on real and synthetic scars on unfailed slopes, it predicts erosion only where terrain shows evidence of it. Using 1 m lidar from before and after the 2018 Hokkaido Eastern Iburi earthquake, cross-validated volumes for 1,708 landslides are within 2.5% of the measured total, with a median per-landslide error of 16%, and 0.1 m spurious depth on unfailed ground. At Iburi and at an independent test site, extending masks to intact ground recovered volumes reliably from a single post-event DTM. We provide the training and testing data in this repository along with the python code for reconstructions.

papers.title: Australia: Political developments and data in 2025 – Labor landslide, Coalition collapse
papers.source: European Journal of Political Research Political Data Yearbook
papers.summary: Abstract This article examines key political developments in Australia during 2025, an election year. The databook entry covers results from the 2025 Landslide re-election of the incumbent Australian Labor Party and their aftermath. Regional elections in two jurisdictions, where both incumbents were returned, as well as a federal Cabinet reshuffle and institutional changes which reformed campaign finance and donations are also discussed. The gender composition of the Federal parliament improved, largely on the back of Labor’s huge majority. The party system faced pressure with the Coalition’s record low election performance, and record performance for Independents and minor parties. National policy issues centred on persistent cost-of-living pressures, including inflation and housing and environmental law reforms. Foreign policy challenges included the Gaza conflict, managing Australia’s relationship with China and continued commitment to the AUKUS submarine programme.

papers.title: A hybrid negative sampling strategy for landslide susceptibility assessment in mining area
papers.summary: Reliable delineation of non-landslide samples remains a challenge in data-driven landslide susceptibility assessment, particularly where landslide inventories are incomplete. This study proposes a hybrid negative sampling (HNS) strategy that integrates frequency ratio (FR)-based susceptibility pre-screening with SPY-based positive–unlabeled (PU) learning and differentiated instance weighting. Specifically, an initial pool of fuzzy negatives was derived from frequency ratio-based susceptibility indices, followed by the SPY algorithm to identify relatively high-confidence negative candidates. The integration of these two sources allows candidate negatives with different screening confidence levels to contribute to model training through distinct weights. Applied to Jiaokou County, a loess mining area in China (157 inventory-positive geological hazard records, 1,914 slope units), the methodology was evaluated using a common five-fold spatial holdout validation protocol with XGBoost and SVM, four baseline sampling strategies, and positive-to-negative ratios of 1:1 and 1:2. HNS achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC across all four classifier–ratio configurations, including 0.812 ± 0.041 for XGBoost and 0.797 ± 0.055 for SVM at 1:2, although its improvements over baseline strategies were modest and not statistically significant. Sensitivity and ablation analyses indicated that differentiated weighting primarily influenced the trade-offs among Recall, Precision, and Specificity, without consistently improving overall discrimination or area-based capture performance. Furthermore, SHAP analysis identified fractional vegetation cover (FVC), nighttime lights (NTL), and lithology as the leading contributors to model predictions rather than direct causal factors. Overall, HNS provides a structured approach to incorporating candidate negatives with different screening confidence levels, offering competitive predictive performance with application-dependent benefits and trade-offs.

papers.title: Slope Units produced from Slope Unit Maker (SUMak) over the contiguous United States, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico
papers.summary: Slope units divide terrain by drainage and divide lines to create mapping units that capture individual hillslopes. Using the software slope unit maker (SUMak) (Woodard, 2023), we delineated slope units across the contiguous United States, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico that are scaled to the fluvial-hillslope threshold (Woodard et al., 2024). Data are organized according to their respective watershed hydrologic unit codes (HUC). The HUC watersheds are designed so that lower-order watersheds (e.g., HUC 4) nest within higher-order watersheds (e.g., HUC 2). The parent directories in this repository are named after the HUC 2 watersheds, and their subfolders are named after the HUC 4 watersheds. Each HUC 4 subfolder contains shapefiles of the delineated stream network, intermediate basins, and slope units. We aggregated all the results of the HUC 8 processed data into one file for each feature within the HUC 4. Shapefiles that show the extent of the HUC watersheds are available at U.S. Geological Survey (2025). Files are named by the HUC 4 code, followed by ‘streams’, ‘intBasins’, and ‘slopeUnits’, for the streams, intermediate basins, and slope units, respectively (e.g., ‘0202intBasins.shp’). papers.title: Occupancy Modelling of Biased Landslide Inventories: When Does Separating Occurrence from Recording Improve on Neutralisation?
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility models are trained on inventories that record where landslides were seen, not where they occurred. The established remedy fits bias-describing variables and neutralises them when mapping. We adapt occupancy-detection modelling from ecology, treating several inventories as imperfect observers of one event and separating occurrence from recording, and ask when this improves on neutralisation. We use near-complete inventories of the 2018 Hokkaido Eastern Iburi, 2015 Gorkha and 2010 Haiti earthquakes with simulated reporting bias, and three real Gorkha inventories. Compared with standard practice, the occupancy model reduces road bias in 24 of 25 paired draws and raises AUC by 0.08-0.14 on Gorkha and 0.03 on Haiti, but only 0.01-0.02 on Iburi. Its median predicted-to-true landslide rate is 0.99 (range 0.44-1.89), against 0.24-0.30 for the baselines. Rescaling the baselines with the same anchor area corrects their median but leaves larger errors (range 0.20-4.34). Cell-level probabilities remain too extreme (calibration slope 0.59). Compared with the best neutralised model, AUC is higher on Iburi (by 0.03-0.07) and lower on Gorkha and Haiti (by 0.01-0.05). Transplant experiments tie the Iburi advantage to the structure of its true landslide pattern, not to its terrain or road network. In all eight settings with a low interaction gap, computable from biased records, neutralisation was at least as accurate, including a prespecified test on Haiti; a high gap did not guarantee an advantage. The real Gorkha inventories are slope-biased, not road-biased, and there the model brings no meaningful gain. Report-based catalogues remain the main untested case.

papers.title: Weather Shocks and Firm Performance: Who Bears the Brunt?
papers.summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between extreme weather exposure and firm performance and whether it differs across development contexts. Using data on 20,518 firms in 102 countries from the 2022–2025 World Bank Enterprise Survey, we exploit a unique firm‐level measure of physical asset damage caused by storms, floods, droughts, landslides and heatwaves. The results show that extreme weather exposure is associated with lower capacity utilisation and annual sales through declines in labour productivity and total factor productivity. At the intensive margin, we find that greater damages are consistently associated with lower sales and labour productivity but not capacity utilisation. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that extreme weather is associated with greater sales losses among firms in middle‐income economies, larger capacity utilisation losses among those in high‐income countries and greatest labour productivity losses in low‐income countries, highlighting heterogeneous climate vulnerabilities across stages of development.

papers.title: Cryohydrologic Flow and Pingo Formation Within Freezing Impact Melts in Occator Crater, Ceres
papers.summary: Ceres is a volatile-rich dwarf planet in the asteroid belt and a potential relict ocean world. It exhibits surface features indicative of subsurface brine activity, particularly within Occator Crater. High-resolution imagery from NASA's Dawn Mission reveals landslides, gullies, carbonate faculae, and mound-like features resembling terrestrial pingos on the floor of Occator Crater. Some of these landforms have been hypothesized to form from water, either from the ascent of deep crustal brines or from the freezeout of impact melt. Here, we test the hypothesis that pingo-like features can be formed via the freezing of shallow impact melts. We simulate the heat transfer and groundwater flow dynamics of a freezing impact melt deposit on the floor of Occator Crater. We test a comprehensive parameter space of regolith physical and material properties relevant to the cerean environment. We find that impact melt freezinf produces pressure gradients sufficient to drive hydrologic flow within the melt matrix and could transport fluids to the near surface through hydraulic fracturing. For most of the parameter space tested, water volumes delivered to pingo candidates on the surface meet or exceed those likely required for pingo formation. Analogous hydrologic processes may be important in the shallow subsurface of other regions of Occator Crater and Ceres at large as well as other ice-rich planetary bodies.

papers.title: LiDAR-Constrained Multi-Temporal UAV Monitoring of Glacier Terminus Retreat and Secondary Landslide Evolution at Hailuogou Glacier, Mt. Gongga, China
papers.summary: Joint quantification of glacier terminus change and adjacent secondary landslide evolution can be challenging when multi-temporal UAV datasets lack a consistent absolute spatial reference, thereby limiting robust assessment of their stage-dependent covariation. This study investigated the Hailuogou glacier terminus and the Laoguanjingtai (LGJT) landslide using six UAV photogrammetric surveys acquired between 2018 and 2022 and synchronous airborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data from 2022. LiDAR reference constraints and elevation-residual assessment over relatively stable terrain supported multi-temporal digital elevation model (DEM) differencing. The glacier terminus area decreased from 2.63×105m2 to 1.43×105m2, representing a reduction of 45.5%. From July 2020 to August 2022, the glacier volume ablation rate reached 1.00×106m3a−1. Meanwhile, the LGJT landslide shifted from deposition-dominated adjustment from 2018 to 2019 to erosion-dominated material export after July 2020, when its erosion rate reached 3.73×105m3a−1 and its net volume change rate decreased to −3.39×105m3a−1. Annualized rates across five unequal intervals showed positive covariation between glacier ablation and landslide erosion and negative covariation with net landslide volume change. These exploratory associations, together with the spatial concentration of elevation change near the glacier–landslide margin, are consistent with a geomorphic linkage. The LiDAR-constrained UAV workflow provides a practical basis for integrated monitoring of glacier retreat and adjacent sediment redistribution.

papers.title: Effects of climate change on hydrogeological hazard: the case of the Niscemi landslides (Southern Sicily, Italy)
papers.summary: Abstract This study analyzes precipitation variability and the hydrometeorological conditions associated with extreme hydrogeological events in the Niscemi area (southern Sicily), combining historical series (1885–2020), ERA5 data, and future projections of rainfall intensity. The comparison between the hydrogeological events of October 12, 1997, and January 26, 2026 highlights how such events can develop through different hydrometeorological configurations, yet are both preceded by high soil moisture conditions, confirming the key role of antecedent precipitation and its temporal distribution. The climatic analysis shows that cumulative precipitation does not exhibit a significant linear trend but is strongly modulated by Euro-Mediterranean atmospheric circulation, with significant negative correlations with EA (ρ = -0.74) and MOI (ρ = -0.66), and more moderate correlations with NAO and WeMO. In contrast, mean rainfall intensity shows an increasing trend over time and is only weakly correlated with the indices, with a significant relationship observed only with WeMO (ρ = -0.34). The intensification is also associated with synoptic configurations characterized by positive NAO. Projections obtained using a SARIMAX model, forced with SSP scenarios, indicate a progressive increase in rainfall intensity throughout the 21st century, reaching up to approximately 40% under high-emission scenarios. Overall, the results highlight that extreme hydrogeological events arise from the interaction between atmospheric circulation variability, thermodynamic conditions, and antecedent rainfall conditions, emphasizing the need for integrated approaches to risk assessment in a climate change context.

papers.summary: Long-term groundwater overexploitation has induced severe land subsidence in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region, while groundwater level rise associated with the South-to-North Water Diversion Project and increased precipitation under climate warming have promoted groundwater level recovery. Rising groundwater levels may alter the hydro-mechanical behavior of thick soft soil and affect the safety of bridge pile foundations in subsidence areas. Taking the bridge pile foundation of the Xiong’an–Daxing rail transit project as an example, this study uses the finite difference method to investigate pile–soil stress and deformation responses under groundwater level rise. A moisture-content-dependent Burgers creep model is established to characterize soil creep and pile–soil interaction. The effects of groundwater level rise induced by groundwater recharge and rainfall on pile foundation deformation, bearing capacity, pore water pressure, and soil settlement are analyzed. The results show that the proposed model captures the staged evolution of soil settlement and that pile bearing capacity responds nonlinearly to groundwater level rise. The findings provide a reference for evaluating the safety of bridge pile foundations and related infrastructure under groundwater level recovery in land subsidence areas.

papers.title: Effects of water content on the mechanical properties of rock and structural planes and slope stability: a case study of a highway rock slope
papers.summary: Abstract To investigate the influence mechanism of water on rock slope stability under different water-content conditions, a high rock slope along a section of the Chongqing–Guizhou Expressway was selected as the engineering case. Initially, field samples were collected and sandstone specimens with varying water content were prepared. Uniaxial compression tests and shear property tests were conducted on natural structural planes within the rock mass to investigate the impact of water on both rock mass specimens and structural planes, while also deeply analyzing the mechanism by which water influences slope instability. Moreover, the slope excavation process under natural and saturated states was analyzed using the 3D-σ three-dimensional finite element numerical simulation software. Herein the stress and displacement variations of the slope during and after excavation were calculated and discussed for different water content states. The results of both physical experiments and numerical calculations demonstrated that: (1) In comparison to the natural state, there was a 23.88% decrease in compressive strength, a 12.34% decrease in elastic modulus, as well as a 21.2% increase in Poisson’s ratio. (2) The deformation of rock mass increases with a higher water content, while its shear strength decreases accordingly. When the rock masses reach a saturated state, there was an observed reduction in shear strength by 11.17%, cohesion decreases by 16.09%, and internal friction angle decreases by 10.02%. (3) The numerical simulation results showed that deformation and stress concentration were closely associated with the weak interlayer, while water saturation amplified the instability response by degrading the mechanical parameters of the slope materials. Compared with the natural condition, the saturated slope exhibited markedly greater shear stress and horizontal displacement during staged excavation. papers.summary: The influence of drying procedures on the pore structure and adsorption performance of graphene quantum dot-modified carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC/GQD) beads for cypermethrin removal has not been sufficiently elucidated. Therefore, hydrogel and cryogel forms of CMC/GQD beads were comparatively evaluated to clarify the effect of oven-drying and freeze-drying on cypermethrin adsorption from aqueous media. Freeze-drying preserved the interconnected porous structure and increased the specific surface area from 7.78 m 2 g -1 for the oven-dried hydrogel to 107.86 m 2 g -1 for the cryogel. Taguchi optimization identified an initial cypermethrin concentration of 90 mg L -1 , pH 6, an adsorbent dosage of 1 g L -1 , and a contact time of 120 min as the optimum conditions. Equilibrium analysis showed that the hydrogel and cryogel were better described by the Langmuir (R 2 = 0.9971) and Freundlich (R 2 = 0.9942) models, respectively, indicating predominantly monolayer adsorption on relatively uniform sites for the hydrogel and heterogeneous, multilayer adsorption for the cryogel. The Langmuir model yielded theoretical maximum adsorption capacities of 174.5 and 296.7 mg g -1 for the hydrogel and cryogel, respectively, while the experimentally determined maximum adsorption capacities were 65.4 and 276.12 mg g -1 , respectively. Kinetic analysis indicated that hydrogel adsorption followed the pseudo-second-order model, whereas cryogel adsorption was described by both pseudo-second-order kinetics and liquid-film diffusion. Thermodynamic analysis confirmed spontaneous and exothermic adsorption, with ΔH° = -86.09 kJ mol -1 and ΔS° = -230 J mol -1 K -1 . The cryogel achieved removal efficiencies of 98.7% in deionized water and 98.6% in simulated agricultural runoff. papers.summary: The high Andean basins of Peru and Ecuador supply freshwater to approximately 60% and 70% of their respective national populations. However, these systems are increasingly threatened by glacier retreat, land-use transformation, and climate variability, which jeopardize long-term water security. This study presents an integrative narrative review of 58 peer-reviewed scientific publications published between 2011 and 2025, focusing on hydrological modeling, cryospheric dynamics, hydrometeorological monitoring, climate change impacts, and ecohydrological processes in tropical Andean mountain systems. Following a systematic selection process, the reviewed evidence was organized into five thematic areas: advances in hydrological modeling under data-scarce conditions, validation of satellite precipitation products, glacio-hydrological and cryospheric dynamics, hydroclimatic scenario simulation, and ecohydrological approaches. The results reveal a sustained methodological transition from semi-distributed conceptual models (SWAT, HEC-HMS, and GR2M) toward physically based distributed models (MGB, PREVAH, and JULES), integrated with satellite products (GPM-IMERG, SM2RAIN, and ERA5-Land) and machine learning algorithms, significantly reducing the limitations associated with data scarcity. Climate projections under CMIP6 scenarios indicate increases of up to 60% in extreme precipitation intensity and up to 39% in annual runoff in some basins, while glacier mass loss could reduce dry-season water storage by as much as 25% over the coming decades. At the same time, land-use changes, including the conversion of páramo ecosystems to pasturelands and deforestation, have been shown to alter baseflow and infiltration processes independently of climatic forcing. The synthesis further reveals that water resilience in the Andes cannot be fully understood through physical hydrology alone. papers.title: Quantitative analysis of urban underground drainage pipeline service status under rainstorm disaster
papers.summary: Abstract Underground drainage pipeline (UDP) system is critical infrastructure for urban flood control and drainage. During extreme rainstorms, rainfall infiltration can alter pore-water pressure and soil-pipe interaction in the surrounding soil. These changes may affect the structural safety of buried pipelines under traffic load. To investigate the structural responses of buried pipelines during extreme rainstorms and provide a basis for emergency assessment, this study integrates full-scale mechanical test, finite element simulation, historical rainstorm scenarios, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) data agent model. Firstly, full-scale pipeline mechanical tests are conducted, and test results are used to calibrate material parameters in numerical simulations; on this basis, a pavement-pipeline coupled numerical model is established to evaluate UDP structural responses under normal service state. Secondly, based on time-series rainfall data from historical rainstorm disaster in Beijing, China, 20 numerical working conditions are established to investigate the effects of pipe voids, burial depth, subgrade soil permeability, and pipeline diameter on structural responses under the coupled action of rainstorm and vehicle load. Finally, a dataset containing 2370 samples is used to develop the 1D-CNN model; this model achieves an MSE of 0.0003 and an R² of 0.9955 on the test set. The proposed framework provides structural response prediction and identifies potentially vulnerable locations, offering a quantitative reference for emergency inspection prioritisation and structural safety assessment of urban pavement-pipeline systems during extreme rainstorms.

papers.title: Submarine groundwater discharge and nutrient enrichment in Kingston Harbour, Jamaica: geochemical evidence and spatial and seasonal dynamics
papers.summary: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) constitutes a critical but systematically underquantified pathway for nutrient delivery to coastal waters, particularly in Small Island Developing States (SIDS) where coastal aquifers may be contaminated by wastewater and urban runoff. This study evaluated spatial and temporal variability in nutrients, chlorophyll a and physicochemical conditions in Kingston Harbour, Jamaica, a coastal water body that has experienced decades of eutrophication and declining biodiversity. This investigation targeted subsurface, low-salinity anomalies consistent with potential fresh SGD (FSGD) which had been identified as a source of land-based pollution in previous studies. Between May 2022 and August 2023, conductivity-temperature-depth (CTD) profiling was conducted to examine potential FSGD sites, along with surface water and targeted-depth water sampling at five northern shore sites which showed recurrent subsurface salinity anomalies. Station blocked permutation tests showed significant temporal variability in all measured surface and targeted depth parameters after Holm adjustment, while date-blocked analyses indicated significant spatial variability in surface waters but not at depth. Paired site-date comparisons did not show systematic enrichment of total oxidized nitrogen (TOxN), total dissolved nitrogen (TDN), soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), total dissolved phosphorus (TDP), soluble reactive silicate (SRSi), chlorophyll a or salinity at targeted depths relative to corresponding surface waters, but depth waters differed significantly from paired surface waters in pH and temperature. Antecedent rainfall was analyzed at the sampling-event level at 1, 3, 5, 7 and 14-day intervals to assess rainfall impacts with the strongest associations observed for 3-day antecedent rainfall with salinity and SRSi. Surface salinity was also significantly associated with multiple nutrient and chlorophyll a variables, including an inverse SRSi-salinity rela

papers.title: Closing the research–practice gap in waterlogging modelling through holistic systems thinking and spatially explicit simulation
papers.summary: Soil waterlogging is a major constraint to global crop production yet remains poorly integrated into agricultural monitoring and decision-support frameworks because waterlogging events are episodic and spatially heterogeneous, while existing modelling approaches largely address individual components of the problem in isolation. We argue that, alongside continued improvement in the representation of key processes, a major and under-addressed bottleneck lies in integrating existing modelling capabilities into an operational decision-support pipeline. Here we propose a conceptual, systems-oriented framework, intended for further development and testing rather than as an implemented decision-support system, that links spatially explicit hazard assessment, crop response simulation and multi-objective evaluation to support adaptation planning. We outline a three-stage modelling pipeline that identifies where and when waterlogging is likely to occur, evaluates alternative engineering, agronomic and genetic interventions, and quantifies trade-offs among productivity, profitability and environmental outcomes. We specify the information exchanged between stages, illustrate the pipeline with a literature-based example, and outline how it could be evaluated and how uncertainty could be handled. Finally, we identify key priorities for advancing waterlogging modelling, including improved process representation of drainage, raised beds, irrigation–groundwater interactions and other adaptation strategies, stronger integration across modelling domains, and closer alignment between modelling outputs and stakeholder needs, beginning with joint framing of the decision problem. By providing a structured pathway for integrating current and future modelling advances into decision support, this framework aims to accelerate the translation of waterlogging research into practical adaptation.

papers.title: Leveraging Biochar to Reduce the Water Footprint in Agriculture: A Comprehensive Review
papers.source: Communications in Soil Science and Plant Analysis
papers.summary: Biochar (BC) has emerged as a soil amendment for improving water retention, enhancing crop productivity, and reducing the agricultural water footprint, particularly in water-limited environments. This review synthesizes current scientific evidence on the role of BC in modifying soil physical, chemical, and hydrological properties that directly influence green, blue, and gray water footprints. BC can modify soil porosity, water-holding capacity (WHC), and field capacity (FC), while influencing bulk density, evaporation, runoff, and deep percolation. These effects can improve plant-available water (PAW) and enhance irrigation water use efficiency (IWUE), potentially reducing the blue water footprint. Improved infiltration, reduced runoff, and enhanced soil aggregation can improve the utilization of effective rainfall and potentially reduce green water footprint. BC can also limit nutrient and contaminant leaching through adsorption and microbial immobilization, potentially reducing the gray water footprint. Synergistic interactions between BC and mulching, micro-irrigation, and conservation agriculture further enhance IWUE and crop water productivity. Crop-modeling tools such as AquaCrop, Soil & Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), and Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) help assess potential BC effects on water productivity and simulate its impacts at both field and watershed scales. Key research gaps include limited availability of long-term field studies, lack of standardized water footprint assessment methods, and insufficient understanding of BC interactions with climatic variability and management practices. Overall, BC shows substantial potential to support sustainable water management and climate-resilient agriculture.Clinical trial number Not Applicable

papers.title: Climate and urban land-use controls on potential groundwater recharge under CMIP6 futures: multi-model uncertainty in a monsoon-dominated urban region
papers.summary: Urban groundwater sustainability depends on how climate change and land-use transformation alter recharge, yet these controls are often assessed separately and with limited representation of climate-model uncertainty. This study developed a 30-m Soil-Water-Balance (SWB2) framework for Sylhet City Corporation, Bangladesh, integrating annual historical land use, FLUS-derived future land use, bias-corrected daily climate forcing from 14 CMIP6 global climate models, parameter-sensitivity experiments, and independent groundwater observations. Potential groundwater recharge was represented by SWB2 net infiltration and evaluated against a 2000–2020 baseline. Historical mean recharge was 517.75 mm yr−1. Under SSP2-4.5, ensemble-mean recharge declined by 16.3–30.9% across four future periods through 2100, while SSP5-8.5 produced reductions of 14.7–22.9%. Recharge remained strongly concentrated in the monsoon season, although all seasons showed future declines. Spatial model-sign analysis identified extensive areas of robust recharge decrease, while substantial inter-model spread persisted in projected magnitudes. Sensitivity experiments showed that recharge was most responsive to curve number and maximum net infiltration, highlighting the importance of land-surface controls on runoff–infiltration partitioning. At the near-boundary groundwater station, recharge anomalies were positively associated with groundwater response at a one-month lag (Spearman ρ = 0.466), with stable leave-one-year-out behaviour. These results demonstrate that future urban recharge emerges from interacting climatic, land-surface, seasonal, and model-structural controls, and that multi-model uncertainty should be explicitly considered when assessing recharge vulnerability in rapidly urbanizing monsoon environments.

papers.title: Optimising Permeable Infrastructure Networks in Sponge City Design for Urban Flood Resilience Using Coupled Hydrological, Clogging and Lifecycle Modelling
papers.summary: Abstract Urban pluvial flooding is intensifying as impervious surfaces expand and extreme rainfall events become more frequent. Sponge city design (SCD) relies on decentralised retention and infiltration, yet planners still lack tools that (i) link the progressive, sediment-driven loss of permeability to maintenance actions, (ii) allocate permeable infrastructure across heterogeneous catchments and (iii) weigh flood-damage savings against lifecycle maintenance costs. This study couples the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) with a Green–Ampt infiltration scheme modified by an exponential sediment-clogging factor and a lifecycle cost–benefit module. Four scenarios were tested on a synthetic 4.5 km² high-density urban catchment under a 50-year, 24-hour design storm: a pipe-only baseline, 30% permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP), 50% permeable infrastructure with bioretention, and an optimised network with subsurface detention and controlled underdrains. The model was calibrated against observed flow data (NSE = 0.88, PBIAS = + 4.2%, RSR = 0.32). The optimised network reduced peak runoff by 43.7% (from 42.6 to 24.0 m³ s⁻¹), reduced total runoff volume by 49.1% and delayed the runoff peak by 68 min. Without maintenance, PICP conductivity fell by 72% within three years, whereas twice-yearly vacuum sweeping sustained about 88% of the initial conductivity. Capital expenditure exceeded that of a conventional upgrade (US$18.4 million versus US$15.5 million), but the discounted payback period was 7.2 years and the 30-year benefit–cost ratio was 2.41; the dominant sensitivities were the flood-damage benefit and the discount rate. The results provide design, maintenance and fiscal guidance for municipal planners moving from reactive to proactive, sponge-city-based drainage planning.

papers.title: Geophysically-informed modelling and interpretation of cosmic-ray neutron sensing response to soil moisture spatiotemporal dynamics
papers.summary: Abstract. Soil moisture and its dynamics have direct hydrological and ecological impacts, from the local field scale to the regional and global scales. Working on a gently-sloping vineyard with grassed interrows, this study combines soil moisture monitoring from cosmic-ray neutron sensing (CRNS) and soil sensors, geophysical characterizations, and CRNS numerical simulations. Multi-scale electrical resistivity tomography and frequency-domain electromagnetic mapping highlight a fingering transition from a clayey substrate to a fractured-karstic marl, both overlain by a more worked and homogeneous soil. Together with ancillary weather data, this spatial information and the associated infiltration dynamics explain how CRNS and nearby soil sensors respond differently to precipitation, depending on season, soil conditions, and rainfall characteristics. This highlights the critical interplay between spatiotemporal soil moisture dynamics and CRNS signal nonlinearity and nonuniqueness. CRNS numerical modelling further investigates this interplay, specifically in terms of lateral dominance of drier regions and amplified sensitivity to moisture changes at the soil surface, here induced by light rainfall events. A theoretical generalization of the dry-dominance is provided, based on Jensen's inequality and a third-order Taylor expansion of the CRNS response function. Together, field observations and numerical modelling inform a conceptual soil hydrology model that describes the observed soil moisture spatiotemporal dynamics. The results reinforce the value of more spatially informed, hydrology-based CRNS applications, a key step toward capitalizing on recent CRNS methodological advances and achieving a better integration with soil moisture networks and multi-methodological hydrological observatories.

Spatiotemporal Responses of Groundwater Levels to Drought–Flood Abrupt Alternation in the Poyang Lake Area: Mechanisms and Multi-Factor Contribution Quantification
papers.summary: Groundwater responses to drought-flood abrupt alternation (DFAA) depend on both rainfall input and antecedent dry-wet conditions. We incorporated the Standardized Drought-Flood Abrupt Alternation Index (SDFAI) into a geographically weighted regression (GWR) model for the Poyang Lake Area. The model performed well (mean local R2 = 0.895). SDFAI showed the largest coefficient-based contribution, accounting for 56.48% under drought-to-flood (DTF) and 56.52% under flood-to-drought (FTD) conditions, compared with 12.36% and 11.64% for precipitation. Despite similar relative shares, the two regimes exhibited contrasting groundwater-response pathways: DTF coefficient patterns were consistent with rapid recharge after antecedent drought and preferential infiltration through clay-rich deposits, whereas FTD coefficient patterns were consistent with delayed aquifer recession and enhanced lateral groundwater discharge as lake stage declined. Alternating SDFAI signs along the lake fringe further indicated a dynamic lake-groundwater hydraulic boundary. SDFAI therefore complements rainfall amount in characterizing groundwater response to abrupt dry-wet transitions.

papers.title: Beyond design performance: hydrological indicators and the effects of rainfall magnitude and facility age on urban green infrastructure
papers.summary: Protocol for a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the hydrological performance of urban green infrastructure (bioretention/rain gardens, permeable pavement, and green roofs). The review (1) synthesises the indicators used to evaluate GI hydrological performance and defines a core indicator set, and (2) pools GI effects on runoff volume, peak flow, and surface infiltration capacity with three-level random-effects models, testing whether these effects decrease with rainfall magnitude and with facility age, and whether reported maintenance moderates the decline with age. Field monitoring and calibrated modelling studies are analysed separately. Web of Science, Scopus, and the Korean Citation Index (KCI) were searched on 11 November 2026; after de-duplication, 9,246 records remain for title/abstract screening, which had not started at registration. Screening uses active learning (ASReview) with the SAFE stopping procedure for Web of Science and Scopus records and manual screening for KCI records. The protocol, search log, export files, and de-duplication script are attached to this registration.

papers.title: Dynamics of inorganic nitrogen cycling, redox conditions, and microbial community composition in a floodplain soil induced by a heavy rainfall after summer drought
papers.summary: Climate change is increasing the frequency of droughts followed by heavy rainfall in temperate regions, with important consequences for water flow, nitrogen transport, redox dynamics, and microbial activity in floodplain soils. We investigated these coupled responses in a field experiment on a fine-textured arable Gleysol after prolonged summer drought. A simulated heavy rainfall event was applied using D 2 O-labeled water as a hydrological tracer, followed by recurrent moderate irrigation with non-labeled water. Soil cores to 50 cm depth were collected from irrigated and dry control plots over 14 d and analyzed for soil water content, δ 2 H signatures, nitrate and ammonium masses, bacterial community composition based on DNA and RNA, and extracellular enzyme activities. In situ redox potentials were monitored along the soil profile. Within two hours after the simulated heavy rainfall, labeled water had reached at least 50 cm depth, indicating rapid preferential flow through drought-induced shrinkage cracks. This was accompanied by a significant decline in nitrate mass in the topsoil without nitrate accumulation at 50 cm depth, suggesting nitrate transport below the investigated profile. In contrast, ammonium remained largely retained and increased only in the uppermost soil layer, consistent with a short-term rewetting-induced mineralization pulse. Subsequent moderate irrigation was retained mainly in the topsoil, likely because shrinkage cracks had closed after initial wetting. Redox potentials declined after irrigation, and were associated with later changes in nitrate pools, although transformation rates were not directly measured. Bacterial community composition remained stable at both DNA and RNA levels, whereas β -glucosidase and exochitinase activities increased after irrigation. Overall, heavy rainfall after drought created a short hydrological window for rapid nitrate displacement through preferential flow pathways, potentially bypassing nitrogen retention

papers.title: Frontier Theories and Practice of the Soil Underground Loss in Karst Areas
papers.summary: Soil underground loss (SUL) is a distinctive erosion process in karst regions, where soil infiltrates into underground conduits through bedrock fissures, posing a severe threat to land resources. This paper reviews the frontier theories and practice of SUL, clarifying its mechanisms driven by soil properties, geomorphological settings, hydrological constraints, and human disturbances such as vegetation destruction and land cultivation. Conceptually, SUL has evolved from a slope-scale subsurface process to a catchment-scale surface–underground continuum, necessitating an integrated definition. Current estimates of SUL’s contribution to total soil erosion vary widely due to methodological and scale discrepancies. Among influencing factors, slope gradient and rainfall intensity consistently emerge as dominant drivers, while fissure degree and rock exposure rate show context-specific effects, highlighting the complexity of factor interactions. Future research should prioritize integrating field tracing with simulation experiments, establishing long-term observation networks, developing process-based models embedding epikarst conduit geometry, and translating findings into targeted mitigation measures. Advancing these directions will provide robust support for rocky desertification control and sustainable land management in karst regions globally.

papers.summary: Abstract. Bedrock moisture plays a crucial role in buffering drought, sustaining vegetation, and recharging groundwater in mountainous landscapes with shallow soils. Stronger weathering is generally assumed to enhance these functions by increasing bedrock water availability. However, our understanding of how weathering regulates the storage, retention, and release of rock moisture is still limited. In this study, using two years of high-frequency moisture observations, we quantified relative water storage, temporal stability, and storage-deficit dynamics across the soil–bedrock continuums of two adjacent hillslopes with contrasting weathering intensities in a representative humid karst catchment. Despite having 21% greater maximum dynamic storage capacity than the weakly weathered hillslope (WWH), the strongly weathered hillslope (SWH) realized only 91.65% of the water storage observed at WWH, indicating that greater storage space did not translate into greater realized storage. Strong weathering promoted rapid infiltration and drainage, thereby reducing bedrock water-storage persistence, as indicated by the faster groundwater recession and less persistent shallow groundwater at the SWH. More importantly, these hydrological contrasts also shaped the responses of the two hillslopes to meteorological drought, with the SWH experiencing a greater decline in water storage than the WWH when annual precipitation notably reduced. This greater sensitivity to reduced rainfall may partly explain the shorter trees and smaller stem diameters observed at the SWH. Accordingly, these results challenge the assumption that stronger weathering could increase water availability, providing key insights into drought resilience, groundwater recharge, and runoff generation in karst critical zones.

papers.title: Quantifying key parameter sensitivities for water table depth in hydrological schemes of CoLM-PSUADE at a mountain forest site
papers.summary: Accurately representing groundwater dynamics in land surface models (LSMs) is crucial for understanding water-energy cycles and assessing water resources. However, most LSMs lack systematic evaluations of parameter sensitivities governing water table depth (WTD) simulations. This study coupled the Common Land Model (CoLM) with Problem Solving environment for Uncertainty Analysis and Design Exploration (PSUADE) in a single-point framework to facilitate systematic parameter analysis and optimization for improving WTD simulation. The soil hydraulic parameter α showed the highest sensitivity. papers.summary: Abstract. Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. papers.summary: Abstract. Forests play a significant role in the hydrological cycle by increasing water use through tree transpiration, reducing soil evaporation, providing local cooling, and altering soil hydrological properties. The nature of these interactions depends on individual tree species’ functional traits, intra- and interspecific interactions, and stand age. In the short term, individuals acclimate to local conditions by adjusting their photosynthetic activity in response to temperature and water availability. As such, over time, changes in forest cover, whether through afforestation or deforestation, will affect water availability in the forest and downstream. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. We verify accuracy, convergence, and strict local mass conservation on two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, and apply the solver to the Lower Murrumbidgee floodplain in New South Wales, Australia. The model covers approximately 30 000 km², contains several hundred million degrees of freedom, and uses public stratigraphic, rainfall, and water-table data. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. papers.title: Assessing machine learning algorithms for prediction of soil infiltration behavior in semi-arid agricultural soils
papers.summary: Accurate estimation of soil infiltration characteristics is fundamental for irrigation design, hydrological modeling, and sustainable soil and water management. However, the nonlinear interactions among soil physical, hydraulic, and chemical properties make reliable prediction of cumulative infiltration (It) and basic infiltration rate (Ib) challenging using conventional statistical approaches. This study evaluated the predictive performance of artificial neural networks (ANNs), random forest (RF), and multiple linear regression (MLR) for estimating It and Ib under three input scenarios of soil properties comprising (i) physical properties, (ii) physical and hydraulic properties, and (iii) physical, hydraulic, and chemical properties. Soil samples were collected from the Bajgah Plain, Fars Province, Iran, and infiltration characteristics were measured using a double-ring infiltrometer. The machine-learning models were trained and tested, and their performance was assessed using different statistical indicators. Among the evaluated models, the double-hidden-layer ANN achieved the highest predictive accuracy (NRMSE = 0.03–0.06, and R 2 = 0.98–0.99) for It using first and second scenarios and for Ib (NRMSE = 0.04–0.06, and R 2 = 0.99) using the first and third scenarios. The RF model also provided highly accurate predictions (NRMSE = 0.045–0.047, and R 2 = 0.96–0.97 for It, and NRMSE = 0.008–0.009, and R 2 = 0.999 for Ib). In contrast, the MLR exhibited the lowest predictive capability (NRMSE = 0.58–0.60, and R 2 = 0.63-066 for It, and NRMSE = 0.77–0.87, and R 2 = 0.27–0.42 for Ib) because of its inability to represent the nonlinear relationships governing infiltration processes. Incorporating saturated hydraulic conductivity improved the prediction of both cumulative infiltration and basic infiltration rate. papers.summary: Widespread anthropogenic alteration of the Earth's surface, especially in vulnerability-sensitive mountain landscapes defines the Anthropocene. This research examines the spatio-temporal dynamics of Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) in Shimla District, Himachal Pradesh, India, over the period 2017–2024, with analyses conducted for the years 2017, 2021, and 2024. The predictions are also calculated and analysed using CA-Markov forecast predicting the dynamics change for 2030 and 2035. High-resolution, multi-temporal Sentinel-2 imagery were considered for the study and analysed using ArcGIS. The supervised classification technique was used to classify the landscape into nine different land use land cover categories. Most strikingly, the results show a significant land expansion in built up area largely at the expense of important ecological buffers. In this time frame, tree cover experienced a loss of around 4%, surface water bodies declined by 25%, and agricultural croplands displayed sporadic but notable reductions of 33% in the same time period up until 2024. Extrapolating into the future, these changes indicate a substantial annualized rate of urban expansion based on the Puyravaud Annual Rate of Change method, which is not sustainable. The study predicts that, with no intervention, a CA-Markov forecast predicts built-up land to reach approximately 750 km² by 2035 will likely lead to additional reductions in both forest and agricultural reserves. The imbalance between development and environmental stability is associated with growing exposure to disasters such as by rainfall-triggered landslide happened in 2023 and 2025 accompanied by seasonal urban water stress. The article critically examines present-day urban policy trajectories and posits sustainable spatial planning as an inevitable mode of Himalayan urbanism for the future.

Vertical Cutoff Walls with Novel Alkali-Activated Slag–Fly Ash Backfills: Hydraulic and Mechanical Behavior
papers.source: Journal of Materials in Civil Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Vertical cutoff walls are widely used as in situ barriers for the containment of contaminated water migration in the subsurface and groundwater. Conventional materials, such as soil–bentonite and soil–cement–bentonite backfill, exhibit the inherent swelling and shrinkage behavior of bentonite, as well as low strength and chemical incompatibility. These characteristics can lead to the development of preferential flow paths, which in turn can reduce long-term containment performance. Hence, in the present study, a novel alkali-activated slag–fly ash (AASF) backfill material was developed for application in the vertical cutoff walls. The workability, hydraulic conductivity, and unconfined compressive strength (UCS) tests of various mixes were evaluated to determine the optimum mix proportions. Further, the hydration products and microstructural development were characterized to elucidate the reaction mechanism underlying the hydraulic and mechanical properties. From the results, the optimum mix proportion is identified to be a mix of 1 ∶ 2 fly ash to ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) with an alkali activator dosage of M1.6N8, having the lowest hydraulic conductivity of 1.3 × 10 − 10 m / s . For a fly ash–to-GGBS ratio of 1 ∶ 2 , with increasing the activator dosage from M1.2N4 to M1.6N8, the hydraulic conductivity is decreased from 1.24 × 10 − 8 to 1.3 × 10 − 10 m / s , and UCS is increased from 10.31 to 28.5 MPa. The highest unconfined compressive strength of 33.28 MPa was observed for the binder with only GGBS and an alkali activator dosage of M1.6N8 at 28 days. From microstructural characterization, a binder ratio of fly ash to GGBS of 1 ∶ 2 , with a modulus of 1.6 and an 8% Na 2 O content, has resulted in the formation of an aluminosilicate gel, which contributes to reduced pore structure and enhanced matric densification.

papers.title: Optimizing Hydraulic-Fracture Networks for Enhanced Thermal Recovery in Single-Well Geothermal Systems: A Coupled Thermo-Hydro-Mechanical (THM) Modeling Study
papers.source: Advances in Applied Mathematics and Mechanics
papers.summary: Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) in hot dry rock (HDR) often require hydraulic stimulation to create permeable flow paths. In naturally fractured reservoirs, hydraulic fractures are strongly guided by pre-existing fractures, shaping connectivity and controlling post-stimulation fluid flow and heat transfer. This study investigates the influence of hydraulic-fracturing parameters on thermal recovery in Single-Well Enhanced Geothermal Systems (SEGS) with natural fractures. A two-dimensional hydraulic-fracturing model is developed using the finite element method (FEM) with zero-thickness cohesive elements to simulate fracture initiation and propagation under the influence of natural fractures. The resulting fracture geometries are embedded into a coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) model to simulate long-term heat extraction. Parametric analyses include fracturing cluster spacing, number of clusters, injection rate, and natural fracture orientation. Results show that cluster spacing affects both fracture geometry and thermal-front evolution: larger spacing promotes longer fractures but may reduce cold-front coverage near the production zone. Natural fracture orientation dominates stimulation effectiveness: larger intersection angles enhance cross-connected networks, increase fluid-rock contact, and improve both heat extraction rate and cumulative production. Increasing the number of clusters shortens individual fractures and intensifies preferential flow along pre-existing fractures, reducing long-term recovery. Higher injection rates enhance fracture propagation and network complexity, enlarging the effective heat-exchange area and strengthening convective heat transfer. By explicitly linking stimulation-induced fracture geometry to subsequent THM heat extraction, this study provides quantitative guidance for optimizing hydraulic-fracturing design in SEGS development.

papers.title: Boosting CO2 Foam Flooding Performance with Tailored CO2-Soluble Fluorinated Surfactants AC18xHFPODA/TA
papers.summary: Abstract CO2 foams generated with water-soluble surfactants are often limited by substantial adsorption losses, poor long-distance transport, and insufficient foam generation in deep reservoir regions. Herein, a series of CO2-soluble fluorinated surfactants, denoted as AC18xHFPODA/TA (where AC = C18 alkyl chain, x = EO chain length, HFPO = hexafluoropropylene oxide oligomer, and DA/TA denote the HFPO dimer and trimer segments, respectively), were synthesized by grafting short-chain fluorinated ether segments derived from hexafluoropropylene oxide oligomers onto an alkylamine polyoxyethylene ether backbone through a molecular hybridization strategy. The chemical structures of the synthesized products were determined by FT-IR, 1H NMR, and 19F NMR spectra. The effects of fluorinated-chain, polyoxyethylene-chain, and alkyl-chain lengths on foaming performance were then systematically evaluated to clarify the relationship between molecular structure and foam-regulating properties. The results showed that incorporation of the fluorinated segments significantly improved CO2 solubility and interfacial activity, while also enhancing adsorption and interfacial stabilization at the CO2/water interface. Among the synthesized surfactants, AC1815HFPODA exhibited the best overall performance, with the critical micelle concentration of 0.158 mmol/L and the corresponding surface tension of 28.68 mN/m (at 25 °C), and the cloud-point pressure of 26.75 MPa with concentration of 2.5 wt % at 50 °C. Core flooding experiments further demonstrated that AC1815HFPODA could comigrate with the CO2 phase and generate stable foams in-situ upon contacting the aqueous phase, increasing the resistance factor to 31.86 and substantially improving CO2 mobility control. papers.title: Al3+ exclusion in macaúba palm diaspores: structural and cytological aspects
papers.summary: Abstract The oil palm macaúba ( Acrocomia aculeata ) maintains seed banks in soils rich in Al 3+ of the Cerrado biome. However, the interaction of this cation with complex diaspores such as those of Arecaceae is still poorly understood. We aimed to evaluate the role of diaspore structure and embryonic cytology in the tolerance of the species’ seeds to Al 3+ . Diaspores (seeds enclosed by the endocarp) were exposed to Al³⁺ (0, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000 and 8000 µM L − 1 ) for 60 days. The histolocalization of Al³⁺ in the seed was performed, and viability, cell membrane functionality, and embryonic respiratory activity were evaluated. Al³⁺ retention by diaspore components was evaluated using quantitative and histochemical methods. Isolated embryos were immersed in the same solutions, and the quantification and histolocalization of Al³⁺ were performed, evaluating its effect on cell structure. Embryo viability and in vitro development were evaluated. The pericarpal structures and the seed coat restrict the penetration of Al³⁺ towards the endosperm and embryo, which maintains the physiological status of the seeds. In embryos, Al³⁺ is retained in the cell walls and also compartmentalized in vacuoles at the periphery of the cotyledon, thus preserving the embryo axis. In vitro development is not affected, and only 8000 µM L − 1 of Al³⁺ reduces embryo viability. Macaúba diaspores are highly tolerant to Al³⁺, exhibiting exclusion mechanisms in both pericarpal structures and embryonic cells. These mechanisms preserve the embryo axis and favor the species’ adaptation to vast regions of the Cerrado biome.

A sequential workflow using fast Fourier transform, Weibull-based updating and lattice Boltzmann method for pore-structure and permeability evolution in digital rocks under hydrostatic strain
papers.source: International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences
papers.summary: Mechanical loading alters rock permeability through changes in pore geometry, but voxel-based digital-rock models lack a direct route from local mechanical fields to an updated pore network. This study develops a one-way sequential workflow integrating fast Fourier transform (FFT)-based homogenization, Weibull-based pore-structure updating, and the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) for digital rocks under prescribed hydrostatic strain loading. FFT-based homogenization first resolves the local stress and strain fields on the initial pore–solid geometry. Candidate interface voxels are ranked by mean compressive stress for closure and maximum principal stress for opening, while Weibull-type cumulative functions prescribe the number of voxel updates along selected porosity-evolution paths. LBM then evaluates the permeability of each updated pore structure. The implementation describes a dry-skeleton, strain-controlled problem: updated geometries are not fed back to the mechanical solver, and pore-pressure/effective-stress coupling is not included. For a 255 3 -voxel Berea sandstone subvolume, the calculated fields localize near pore–matrix interfaces and narrow solid ligaments, producing spatially selective pore updates. The normalized permeability decreases to 0.8314 at ɛ 0 = − 0 . 0 1 and increases to 1.2199 at ɛ 0 = 0 . 0 1 . Comparison with a normalized Kozeny–Carman-type relation gives mean absolute percentage errors of 0.64% for compression and 1.17% for tension. The remaining differences reflect three-dimensional pore-throat and connectivity changes that cannot be represented by porosity alone. The workflow therefore links prescribed hydrostatic strain, mechanically ranked pore updates, and permeability without claiming iterative hydromechanical coupling or direct simulation of damage and fracture.

Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management. papers.title: Morphometry and Development of Alluvial Fans in the Caserta Plain, Southern Italy
papers.summary: Three generations of slope, colluvial, and alluvial fan systems indicated with F1, F2, and F3, respectively, distributed along the Tifatini Mountains front, at the northeastern margin of the Campanian Plain, southern Italy, were investigated. Field observations, stratigraphic data, geomorphological mapping, DTM-based morphometry, hypsometric analysis, and log–log scaling relationships were integrated to define the morphometric and sedimentological characteristics of the F1, F2, and F3 fan systems. F1 consists of small, steep, and incised fans close to the mountain front and strongly controlled by the tectonic activity. F1 deposits are mainly related to debris-flow and debris-flood processes. F2 includes intermediate piedmont fans characterized by more weak morphometric coupling with the source basins and by a greater role of sediment reworking, producing colluvial fan deposits. Climate was the main factor in controlling these fans than tectonics. F3 consists of large, low-gradient fans developed farther of basins source, where sheetflood and streamflow processes, volcaniclastic aggradation, and subsidence appear to have been dominant. A chronological framework was proposed by comparing the fan systems with the post-15 ka NGRIP δ18O curve, the pollen assemblage zones of the Lago Grande di Monticchio, and the main Campanian volcanic events. F1 was tentatively assigned to the Younger Dryas and the Monticchio PAZ 2, F2 to the Early Holocene minor climatic oscillations, combined with pyroclastic inputs, whereas F3 was related to Mid- to Late-Holocene volcaniclastic supply. Although direct numerical ages are not available, the results suggested a control of tectonics, climate, and volcanoclastic sediment supply on the geomorphic connectivity of the three fan systems.

papers.title: Evaluating DEM Refinement Strategies and Flow-Depth Threshold Criteria for Debris Flow Simulation in a Data-Limited Catchment
papers.summary: Debris flows can severely damage downstream areas, but predicting their impacts is often hindered by coarse topographic data. This study evaluates whether digital elevation model (DEM) refinement improves debris flow simulations in a data-limited catchment using the Hyper KANAKO system. It also examines whether flow-depth threshold analysis provides a more standardized basis for interpreting simulation results. Three DEM configurations were evaluated using a documented debris flow event in South Korea: (1) incorporation of building elevations, (2) refinement of channel and road topography, and (3) a combination of both approaches. Simulated areas were compared with the observed affected area using receiver operating characteristic (ROC)-based performance measures and confusion matrix indices. Refinement of channel and road topography (DEM configuration 2) yielded the most consistent improvement, with an accuracy of 0.961 and the highest F1 score (82.6%). Flow-depth threshold analysis identified 0.3 m as a practical threshold for delineating deposition-area boundaries across the DEM configurations. When both overprediction and underprediction were considered, Case 2, which applied the ROC-derived, application-specific threshold (Youden’s J cut point), achieved the highest Net Success Index. The proposed workflow offers a potentially transferable approach to debris flow hazard mapping and erosion-control planning in areas where high-resolution topographic data are unavailable.

papers.title: Turbiditic sedimentation during syn-orogenic evolution of the Paleoproterozoic Nûkavsak Formation (Karrat Group), West Greenland
papers.summary: The Karrat Group extends hundreds of kilometers along the Rae craton of coastal West Greenland and represents deposition prior to and during Paleoproterozoic orogenic events. The Nûkavsak Formation, the youngest stratigraphic unit of the Karrat Group, preserves sedimentary structures that facilitate the reconstruction of depositional environments, despite tectonic deformation. Here, the sedimentary facies, depositional environments, and tectonic setting of the Nûkavsak Formation are addressed while also considering contextual information from detrital zircon provenance analysis and underlying strata. Our analysis delineates seven lithofacies within the Nûkavsak Formation. The depositional setting reflects variations in water depth, proximity to sediment sources, and tectonic activity. The formation was deposited below storm wave base through cohesive and turbulent sediment gravity flows, debris flows, and hemipelagic sedimentation. Deposition in a retro-arc foreland system explains the overall setting and aligns with sedimentological observations. Defining the stratigraphic architecture and facies analysis of the Nûkavsak Formation highlights similarities and differences with Paleoproterozoic sedimentary successions in eastern Arctic Canada and West Greenland that were deposited within the context of the Rinkian and Trans-Hudson orogens.

papers.title: Fallback Rates in Tidal Disruptions: How Far Below the Density and Shear Ceilings the Returning Debris Flows
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This paper computes a grid of black hole masses from 10^5 to 10^8 solar masses disrupting a solar-type star and compares the resulting quantities with the density and shear ceilings set by the Aldred Limit on the neutron branch, rho_A = 9.72e54 g per cubic centimetre. For a black hole of a million solar masses disrupting a solar-type star, the fallback time is 41.0 days and the peak fallback rate is 2.97 solar masses per year. Across the full set of cases examined, the astrophysical quantities remain separated from the ceilings by margins of tens of orders of magnitude, so the ceilings do not participate in the dynamics of these events; their role is that of an audit scale against which claimed extremes can be checked arithmetically. All values are computed from stated assumptions and published event properties. This study is simulated and computed, not measured.

Effect of Varieties and Planting Conditions on Key Volatile Components of Virgin Olive Oil Based on Gas-Phase Ion Mobility Spectrometry Technology
papers.summary: Analyzing 30 virgin olive oil samples from 15 planting sites, our results suggest that both variety and environment were associated with the volatile compositions observed. Specifically, ‘Laixing’ tended to accumulate higher aldehyde levels than ‘Ezhi No. 8’ under identical conditions, whereas ‘Ezhi No. 8’ showed a higher proportion of esters and alcohols. Notably, debris-flow alluvial fan soils were associated with a higher relative share of aldehydes in ‘Laixing’; because aroma-precursor pools were not measured, this is stated at the level of the volatile profile. Our results suggest that, in this dataset, varietal differences were apparent and environmental conditions were associated with distinct volatile metabolome patterns; however, cultivar and environment effects could not be fully decoupled in this sampling design. Because the site-level contrasts were based on single composite samples with technical replicates only, these findings should be regarded as exploratory; they nonetheless offer a preliminary reference for guiding regional cultivation strategies toward olive oils with distinct flavor profiles, pending confirmation in future replicated trials.

papers.title: Oil Content and Mobility of Xiaganchaigou Formation in Yingxiongling Area, Qaidam Basin: Dominant Lithofacies and Controlling Factors
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Mixed shale represents an important target for shale‐oil exploration in lacustrine basins. However, its strong heterogeneity leads to pronounced variations in shale‐oil content and mobility. Therefore, identifying favorable lithofacies and clarifying their controlling factors are critical for shale‐oil sweet spot exploration. In this study, lithofacies of the Xiaganchaigou Formation in the Yingxiongling area, Qaidam Basin, were classified on the basis of mineral composition and subsequently evaluated using geochemical, pore structure, brittleness, and fracability characteristics. Mixed shale is volumetrically dominant, whereas calcareous shale exhibits more favorable oil content and mobility and is identified as the most favorable lithofacies within the studied interval. The controlling factors of shale‐oil content differ from those of mobility among different lithofacies. Shale‐oil content is mainly controlled by shale thickness, organic matter abundance, and thermal maturity, whereas mobility is primarily influenced by fracability, mineral composition, and pore structure. Favorable lithofacies are, therefore, characterized by the coupled effects of organic matter abundance, mineral composition, pore structure, and fracability. These findings provide a basis for shale‐oil sweet spot evaluation and target optimization in the Xiaganchaigou Formation of the Yingxiongling area.

papers.summary: This repository provides a compact worked example of the thin-flow seismic inversion used for Fig. 5 of Gheri et al., Multi-sensor geophysical observations constrain lahar dynamics remotely at Volcán de Fuego, Guatemala (manuscript under review). The example reproduces the FGL1 model-derived effective coarse-particle diameter, D73, following the physical formulation of Farin et al. (2019). The repository includes a calibrated FGL1 miniSEED waveform, the inversion notebook, and the Python functions required to compute RMSA, the seismic coupling term gr0, and the thin-flow inversion. The complete multi-sensor dataset used in the study is publicly available through the associated Scientific Data Data Descriptor and Zenodo archive (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19683587). References Farin, M., Tsai, V. C., Lamb, M. P., & Allstadt, K. E. (2019). A physical model of the high-frequency seismic signal generated by debris flows. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms, 44(13), 2529–2543. Gheri, D., De Angelis, S., Pineda, A., Woodhouse, M., & Phillips, J. (2026).
