papers.title: Re-Evaluation of Bermuda Triangle Hypothesis on Physical, Hydrodynamic, and Geophysical Analysis of Vortex Dynamics in the Western North Atlantic
papers.source: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.summary: This paper presents a formal fluid dynamic and transport phenomena evaluation of the relationship between force mechanisms and vortex motion in the western North Atlantic. It is a domain conventionally designated as the Bermuda Triangle. The study rigorously evaluates whether empirical or theoretical physical evidence supports the existence of unique, localized forces or supernatural vortex phenomena capable of causing maritime and aviation disappearances. Applying foundational principles of continuum mechanics, geophysical fluid dynamics, and atmospheric dynamics, the paper had model canonical vortex structures including forced, free, and Rankine combined vortices and scale them against natural rotational flows such as mesoscale ocean eddies and tropical cyclones. Furthermore, the investigation addresses critical physical gaps frequently omitted from traditional literatures, defining mathematical formulations for surface wind stress vectors, two-phase methane hydrate ebullient density reductions, non-linear Schrödinger rogue wave interactions, microburst downburst mechanics, and agonic geomagnetic drift dynamics. Mapping these mathematical formulations directly to historical incidents confirms that open-ocean boundary conditions cannot sustain stationary, macro-scale forced vortices or downward hydrodynamic suction fields. Instead, vessel disappearances and the absence of wreckage are fully described by Rankine storm-core turbulence, non-linear wave slamming, buoyancy destabilization, and rapid debris advection along the Gulf Stream's high-velocity vector (𝑉𝑚𝑎𝑥 > 2.5 m/s). In conclusion, while multi-physics environmental force vectors create hazardous operational conditions, no anomalous physical forces exist within the region and there is no scientifically verified evidence of localized or supernatural vortex forces. Observed losses align strictly with standard statistical risk distributions in heavily navigated, high-energy transport corridors.

papers.title: Critical Initiation Mechanism and Multi-Field Response Characteristics of Coal Gangue Debris Flow Under Different Slope Angles
papers.summary: Coal gangue deposits may develop debris flows under hydraulic loading, yet how slope angle affects initiation and internal responses remains unclear. Flume experiments were conducted using coal gangue from western Beijing at 12°, 16°, 20°, and 24°, with large-scale particle image velocimetry, pore-water pressure, earth pressure, and MEMS measurements. Coupled PFC–FiPy simulations at 16°, 20°, and 24° examined particle motion, stress, porosity, and seepage. Initiation was progressive and spatially asynchronous, evolving from localized rolling and sliding to widespread sustained movement. Critical initiation discharges were approximately 132.19, 42.56, 59.00, and 29.10 m3/h, respectively, showing an overall decline with increasing slope angle despite a higher threshold at 20° than at 16°. Simulated high-velocity zones initially developed near the slope toe and extended inward, with maximum local particle velocities of approximately 0.347, 0.387, and 0.412 m/s, respectively. Pore-water pressure and effective saturation were relatively high near the toe, while vertical stress and porosity varied spatially. The findings suggest that increasing slope angle generally favors initiation by increasing downslope gravitational loading and reducing normal constraints, while local seepage and particle-contact variability may affect instability propagation. These findings support debris-flow hazard assessment and monitoring at coal gangue disposal sites.

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-5979
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow numerical models are widely used for hazard assessment and engineering design, yet many models still treat bed evolution in a simplified or uncoupled manner. This study presents faDebrisFOAM, an open-source depth-averaged solver developed in OpenFOAM® that couples debris-flow motion, entrainment, deposition, and terrain evolution within a finite-area framework. The model represents the mixture as an equivalent fluid of variable density and incorporates mass exchanges with an erodible bed layer through entrainment and deposition laws. The Terrain Modification Algorithm (TMA), developed in this work, updates the computational grid at each time step, allowing topographic changes to feed back directly into the governing equations and simulated flow dynamics. The model is evaluated through three applications: validation against large-scale US Geological Survey (USGS) flume experiments, testing in an idealized parabolic geometry, and application to the 2015 debris-flow event in the La Mesilla catchment in northern Chile. The solver reproduces the measured evolution of flow thickness in the USGS flume experiments with good agreement. The idealized application demonstrates that terrain evolution is not a passive output but an active control on run-out, velocity, flow depth, and volume redistribution. The La Mesilla case further shows that coupled terrain modification promotes surge self-generation, self-channelization, and channel-plug formation, which are absent or weakened when the TMA is disabled. These results indicate that coupled terrain evolution can modify flow confinement, stress distribution, and preferential routing throughout the simulation. faDebrisFOAM therefore provides an open-source framework for investigating morphodynamic feedbacks in debris-flow propagation.

papers.title: Hydro-Mechanical Analysis of Cylindrical Cavity Expansion in Unsaturated Soils Under Constant Total Vertical Stress
papers.summary: Radial soil displacement during pile installation and pressuremeter testing is commonly interpreted using cylindrical cavity expansion theory. However, conventional plane strain solutions neglect vertical deformation and may be inadequate for unsaturated ground subjected to approximately constant overburden stress. This study develops a semi-analytical elastoplastic solution for cylindrical cavity expansion under constant total vertical stress. An unsaturated modified Cam-Clay model and a soil-water retention relationship are incorporated within a skeleton stress framework, while vertical deformation is explicitly considered in radial equilibrium. Coupled first-order governing equations are established for undrained and constant-suction drained conditions. The formulation agrees with an existing saturated drained solution in the limiting case. For the initial stress states examined, increasing overconsolidation ratio is associated with higher cavity pressure at a given expansion ratio but a smaller expansion ratio at which the cavity wall reaches the critical state. For normally consolidated soil, the corresponding ratios are 1.203 (undrained) and 1.375 (constant-suction drained). Under undrained conditions, changes in suction and saturation cause the vertical skeleton stress to evolve despite constant total vertical stress. The proposed framework provides a theoretical basis for evaluating cavity-induced soil disturbance and stress redistribution relevant to foundation construction in unsaturated ground.

papers.summary: This record contains the data, supplemental tables, and analysis code for a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the accuracy of low-cost and research-grade soil water content sensors. The study pooled 488 root-mean-square error (RMSE) values from 31 peer-reviewed studies to estimate typical sensor accuracy and its spread at new sites. It examined how accuracy depends on the calibration route (factory equation, generic, or soil-specific calibration), on the data used to evaluate a calibration (fitting or independent data), on sensor cost class, on test setting, and on soil texture. It also expressed the pooled errors as a fraction of the readily available water used in irrigation scheduling, and as changes in suction stress and the factor of safety of an unsaturated slope. papers.title: Antecedent rainfall effects on the stability of soil‒rock mixture slopes: influence of matrix type and volumetric block proportion
papers.summary: The antecedent-rainfall effects on soil–rock mixture (SRM) slope stability remain poorly quantified. This PLAXIS 3D study tracks displacement, pore water pressure (PWP), and factor of safety (FOS) through a six-stage antecedent rainfall sequence (−72 to +72 h; peak 0.134 m/day) across 12 configurations: three USDA matrices (Loamy sand, Sandy loam, and Silty loam) at volumetric block proportions (VBP) of 0%, 15%, 25%, and 35%. The model was benchmarked against centrifuge, physical-model, and field-monitoring studies of unsaturated and block-in-matrix slopes, and its sensitivity to rainfall intensity and duration, water-table depth and matrix strength was assessed. FOS was maximized within a narrow band, at 15% VBP in every matrix. Displacement and stability dissociated: Sandy loam at 35% VBP gave among the smallest peak-rainfall displacements (0.002 m) yet a lower FOS than at 15%, so displacement alone can understate risk. Loamy sand failed (FOS < 1.0) at 0% and 35% VBP. Localized positive-PWP cells around blocks, termed water patch zones, formed preferential failure paths. After peak rainfall, FOS fell for 72 h in Sandy and Silty loam, while Loamy sand displacement and PWP kept rising. From one geometry and one event, the VBP thresholds are model-based indicators for monitoring and field verification, not design values.

papers.source: Fatigue & Fracture of Engineering Materials & Structures
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Freeze–thaw cycling and cyclic disturbance jointly affect rock stability in cold‐region mines, yet their influence on sandstone damage evolution remains insufficiently understood. Sandstone from the Dasuji Molybdenum Mine underwent 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40 freeze–thaw cycles, followed by uniaxial compression and cyclic disturbance tests at 5 Hz. Acoustic emission (AE), RA‐AF analysis, X‐ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy characterized damage evolution and cracking behavior. Freeze–thaw cycling progressively reduced both peak strength and elastic modulus. Cyclic disturbance promoted propagation and coalescence of existing defects. Recorded peak AE energy and ringing counts generally declined, while the proportion of shear‐classified AE events increased from 31.2% to 53.6%. Major mineral composition remained largely unchanged, whereas pore expansion, intergranular debonding, and fracture development indicated progressive microstructural deterioration. These results provide experimental insights into sandstone damage evolution relevant to slope stability assessment in cold‐region mines.

papers.title: Constraining Subsurface Connectivity by Water‐Trace Experiment in Deep, Semi‐Arid Karst Terrain
papers.summary: Abstract This pilot water‐trace experiment evaluates subsurface hydraulic connectivity between an ephemeral channel and a deep fractured‐carbonate aquifer (vadose zone thickness >300 m) to assess managed aquifer recharge (MAR) feasibility in semi‐arid settings. The study site comprises an ephemeral channel incised into fractured limestone, selected for its documented infiltration capacity and proximity to structural lineaments expected to enhance vertical permeability through the deep unsaturated zone. The primary objective was to constrain groundwater flowpaths and transit times under controlled low‐flow recharge conditions relevant to MAR operations. Rhodamine WT tracer was introduced via continuous reclaimed water outflow at approximately 0.95 m 3 /min (250 gpm) over 48 h. Monitoring was conducted at two downgradient municipal wells and one upgradient site using passive charcoal receptors, water grab samples, and continuous in‐situ fluorometry. While measured concentrations were below standard quantitative detection thresholds, contemporaneous anomalous fluorescence signals were observed at a municipal production well (2.7 km downgradient) by two independent methods 11‐13 d after dye introduction, yielding an apparent groundwater velocity of approximately 200‐250 m/d. No detection occurred at the further downgradient municipal well or upgradient site. The results provide preliminary evidence of rapid subsurface connectivity in this fractured‐carbonate system. The transit time and flowpath geometry have important implications for MAR design, particularly regarding residence time and water quality. This study demonstrates that controlled water‐tracer introduction coupled with redundant detection methods can constrain connectivity in semi‐arid karst‐matrix aquifers and provides a transferable methodological framework for MAR feasibility evaluation.

papers.title: A unified model embedding MCC-MLD constitutive laws in Biot’s framework for settlement of Weinan interbedded clay-sand loess foundations
papers.summary: Consolidation settlement prediction in interbedded clay–sand loess foundations is complicated by stratigraphic heterogeneity and hydromechanical coupling that homogeneous-soil models cannot capture. This study presents an integrated elastoplastic framework combining the Modified Cam-Clay model for loessial clay, the Wright–Duncan model for sand with particle breakage, and Biot’s consolidation theory in a unified implementation for the Weinan plain, China. Parameters for clay, sand, and transitional interlayers came from 20 borehole samples. Although each component is established, their integration with site-specific enhancements—a structure-dependent yield surface for shallow clay and a breakage-dependent hardening law for deep sand—constitutes a practical advancement. The numerical implementation via Python-Matlab, validated against borehole data from the same site using a reserved validation set (6 boreholes not used in calibration), reveals settlement in three stages—elastic rebound, primary consolidation (70–80% of total), and secondary creep—peaking at the 20–30 m clay–sand interface, where sand dilatancy transfers 12–18% of stress to clay, quantified by the proposed γ–μ interface parameter system. Spatially, settlement is shallow-dominated with deep-layer lag; temporally, sand accelerates clay pore-pressure dissipation by 35–40%. The model attains ± 5% accuracy versus ± 25% for homogenization and establishes a closed-loop monitoring–inversion–updating workflow. Assuming full saturation, it neglects matric-suction effects in the vadose zone, including water-table fluctuations and dry–wet cycles. At the Weinan site (water table 15–25 m), the model applies directly to deep saturated strata, contributing most (70–80%) of consolidation settlement; the shallow unsaturated zone requires caution and further characterization.

Field monitoring demonstrates that horizontal displacements respond sensitively to construction sequences, while building-settlement responses develop over several days to about one week after the corresponding construction stage. Integrating susceptibility and effective rainfall thresholds for regional landslide warning in Wushan
papers.summary: This study delves into the early warning system for regional rainfall-induced landslide hazards. By integrating landslide susceptibility mapping and critical rainfall thresholds, a spatiotemporal probabilistic prediction framework for landslide hazards is established. Taking Wushan County as the study area, the authors utilised 313 recorded rainfall-triggered landslide events and meteorological rainfall data spanning from 2010 to 2024. Initially, a landslide susceptibility prediction model was constructed using the Random Forest algorithm, with model accuracy validated by the area under the curve (AUC) metric (AUC = 0.85). Subsequently, critical rainfall thresholds were determined through a comprehensive analysis of antecedent effective rainfall, employing three models: effective rainfall intensity-duration (EI-D), cumulative effective rainfall-duration (EE-D), and cumulative effective rainfall-effective rainfall intensity (EE-EI). Finally, a landslide hazard warning map was generated by spatially superimposing susceptibility classifications and rainfall threshold exceedance probabilities, accompanied by corresponding disaster prevention strategies. The results demonstrate that this integrated methodology enhances the precision of regional landslide early warnings, as supported by quantitative validation metrics (probability of detection = 0.76, true skill statistic = 0.44), providing a scientifically robust decision making framework for natural resource management authorities in disaster risk mitigation.

papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility identifies terrain associated with landslide occurrence, whereas risk prioritization also requires information on the vulnerability of threatened elements. This letter presents a slope-unit framework linking machine-learning susceptibility prediction, SHAP-based interpretation, and vulnerability-based relative risk classification. Four models were evaluated using a regional test dataset, and the selected model was applied to 393 slope units. XGBoost achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC = 0.952), followed by random forest (0.904), logistic regression (0.662), and support vector machine (0.600). Paired DeLong tests indicated significant differences between XGBoost and logistic regression (LR) and support vector machine (SVM), but not random forest (RF). SHAP analysis identified slope, relief, and elevation as the leading predictors, accounting for 62.83% of normalized grouped importance. High and very high relative risk occupied 21.34% of the mapped slope-unit area. Of 69 very-high-susceptibility units, only 13 were classified as very high risk after vulnerability integration. The framework supports the identification of priority slope units for targeted field investigation, monitoring, and mitigation planning.

papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.summary: Research concerning the chain effects and disaster mechanisms of landslides resulting from the combined influences of goaf and mining blasting is lacking. Goaf and mining blasting represent typical artificial disturbances that affect mine slopes. This paper focuses on the Jiweishan landslide in Wulong, Chongqing, as the primary case study. Through comprehensive geological investigation, numerical simulation, and theoretical analysis, the landslide disaster mechanism influenced by the combined effects of goaf and mining blasting was systematically examined. In this study, UDEC software was used to reveal the failure mechanism of Jiweishan landslide under the combined effects of goaf and mining blasting by using the global block discrete element method in the numerical model. Following the formation of extensive goaf areas from mining, the overlying strata lost support, resulting in uneven settlement. The potential sliding mass tended to experience slight subsidence and lateral deformation. The prescribed blasting input promoted progressive failure in the excavated slope model. Under the given blasting wave input, the Jiweishan landslide exhibited a progressive advancing failure trend: tensile fractures first initiated and developed at the trailing edge of the landslide. As the blasting process continued, the fractures at the rear edge expanded, extended, and connected, whereas the anti-sliding performance of the front-edge locking section progressively deteriorated. Ultimately, the entire front-edge sliding mass was sheared off, resulting in a debris flow disaster. The findings inform sustainable mining practice by highlighting the need to account for goaf-induced deformation in pre-blast slope assessments and by identifying priorities for long-term monitoring, including crack opening at the rear and displacement in the middle and at the front locking segment.

papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.summary: Abstract A case study analyzing three landslides in Pohang, South Korea, during tropical storm Typhoon Hinnamnor in September 2022 is conducted to assess the suitability of the recently developed suction stress–based rainfall intensity–duration (SS-ID) paradigm for predicting multiple slope instabilities. Postfailure field investigation and laboratory testing were carried out to determine field hydrologic and geotechnical settings and soil properties. This information was used to determine these slopes’ critical suction stress profiles where the effective stress reaches the failure state or the local factor of safety reaches unity. Hydromechanical numerical modeling was then conducted under various rainfall intensities to identify the slopes’ corresponding durations for slope failure and thus the rainfall intensity–duration (ID) threshold curves of the slopes. The precipitation records during and before Typhoon Hinnamnor at Pohang were used to determine rainfall episodes and slopes’ rainfall intensity–duration data. The determined rainfall intensity–duration data at the three sites for Typhoon Hinnamnor were all above the corresponding predetermined ID threshold curves, correctly and novelly predicting the occurrence of the observed landslides. Further independent physical simulations of transient two-dimensional hydromechanical processes at the three failed slopes were conducted for independent confirmation. Excellent matches in predictions of the slope failure locations and timings are demonstrated, further physically validating the suitability and effectiveness of the SS-ID paradigm for multiple slope instability prediction. Because the suction stress–based ID curves are characteristic of a given region and they can be determined a priori, the SS-ID paradigm provides a practical way to use live rainfall data to forecast multiple slope instability in a region.

papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.summary: Conventional approaches for preliminary rock slope assessment lack precision, as they omit critical parameters related to slope geometry and failure mechanism, whereas comprehensive numerical analyses are computationally demanding. This study develops a surrogate modeling framework for rapidly predicting the performance of rock slopes governed by both rock mass and discontinuity-controlled failures. A synthetic database comprising 10,041 FEM/LEM models and 90,658 outputs was generated across five rock mass quality classes, three discontinuity classes, and systematically varied slope geometries representing a wide range of slope configurations. Mass failures were analyzed using shear strength reduction and limit equilibrium methods, while planar sliding, wedge failure, and block and flexural toppling were evaluated using limit equilibrium analyses. The resulting factor of safety, maximum total displacement, and maximum shear strain values were used to train feed-forward neural networks. The models achieved an average correlation coefficient of 0.96 for the factor of safety predictions of mass failures, while coefficients of 0.97 and 0.89 were obtained for maximum total displacement and maximum shear strain, respectively. Planar and toppling predictions also yielded an average correlation of 0.96. Independent benchmark cases produced an average coefficient of determination of 0.95, excluding wedge failure. Wedge predictions showed lower performance because valid wedge formation depends on restrictive combinations of discontinuity dip and dip direction. The proposed framework can efficiently screen extensive design spaces and identify critical scenarios based on detailed numerical investigation. The proposed method provides a computationally efficient preliminary assessment tool for slopes while explicitly accounting for multiple failure mechanisms.

papers.summary: Abstract Reservoir-level variations associated with hydropower operation can alter the hydraulic and mechanical response of adjacent slopes, while evidence linking these processes to numerical modeling remains dispersed across operational scenarios and methods. The objective of this study is to integrate the available evidence on reservoir-slope response to water-level variations through bibliometric analysis and systematic technical synthesis, examining operational hydraulic scenarios and the capabilities, applicability, and limitations of numerical and hydro-mechanical modeling approaches. The methodology comprised three phases: (i) literature search and bibliographic corpus construction; (ii) bibliometric analysis and science mapping; and (iii) systematic review and comparative technical synthesis. The search retrieved 479 records; thematic refinement yielded 420 records for bibliometric analysis, and systematic screening retained 163 studies for technical synthesis. Bibliometric analysis showed recent growth and thematic emphasis on rapid-drawdown stability assessment and numerical modeling of reservoir-level fluctuations. The technical synthesis showed that reservoir-level variation does not produce a unique mechanical response; stability depends on the transient balance between external hydrostatic support and internal hydraulic response, conditioned by permeability, drainage, geometry, structural controls, and hydraulic history. Hydraulic lag was identified in 77.9% of studies. Model applicability depended on the failure mechanism, material domain, deformation regime, and engineering output rather than on a universal hierarchy of methods. Formal geotechnical uncertainty analysis of model inputs and spatial variability was reported in only 9.2% of studies. Overall, reservoir elevation or drawdown rate alone cannot define slope condition, and model complexity should be matched to the process and engineering output of interest.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards in the Himalayan region of India, causing substantial damage to infrastructure, natural resources, and local communities. This study presents an integrated hydro-geotechnical approach for regional landslide susceptibility assessment by combining statistical susceptibility mapping with slope stability evaluation. The proposed framework considers the influence of key hydrologic factors, including rainfall, drainage density, topographic wetness, and groundwater conditions, together with geotechnical properties to better explain the mechanisms controlling slope failure. Five bivariate statistical models, namely, frequency ratio (FR), information value (IV), weight of evidence (WoE), certainty factor (CF), and Shannon entropy (SE), were applied to produce landslide susceptibility maps. Their performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) and landslide density index (LDI). Among the evaluated models, SE achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( AUC = 87.17 % ), followed closely by FR (87.06%). The results indicate that steep slopes ( > 30 ° ), weak lithological formations, high drainage density, and groundwater conditions are the main factors controlling landslide occurrence in the study area. Slope stability was further evaluated using laboratory-derived geotechnical parameters and circular failure charts (CFC), providing an independent assessment of slope conditions under different groundwater scenarios. The combined use of statistical modeling, hydrologic factors, and geotechnical verification improves the reliability of landslide susceptibility assessment and provides a practical framework that can be applied in other mountainous regions affected by rainfall-induced landslides.

papers.summary: Sawangan District in Magelang Regency is an area prone to landslides due to topographic conditions and environmental characteristics that facilitate their occurrence. Situated between Mount Merapi and Mount Merbabu, the region features varying slope gradients, unconsolidated volcanic materials, and relatively high rainfall. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility levels for 2025 and the probability of landslide occurrence in Sawangan District during the 2024–2025 period. A descriptivequantitative method was employed, utilizing a spatial analysis approach specifically overlay and scoring techniques alongside binary logistic regression analysis to determine landslide probability values. Sampling was conducted using a purposive sampling method based on five environmental parameters and recorded landslide locations. The research results indicate that Sawangan District is categorized into four landslide susceptibility classes: not susceptible, slightly susceptible, susceptible, and highly susceptible. Binary logistic regression analysis reveals that landslide probability falls into four classes low, moderate, high, and very high, with an AUC value of 0.846, demonstrating the model's good discriminative ability in distinguishing between landslide and non-landslide locations. While landslide occurrences are predominantly found in the susceptible and highly susceptible classes, some incidents also occurred in the slightly susceptible and not susceptible classes. These findings indicate that landslides can occur across various levels of susceptibility and slope gradients; therefore, vigilance is required not only in areas with high susceptibility but also in those with lower susceptibility. Overlay analysis reveals a link between susceptibility and landslide probability, though the two do not always exhibit a direct, consistent relationship

papers.summary: The conversion of forest land to agricultural land can alter vegetation cover and affect slope stability. This study aims to identify changes in land cover and map landslide risk levels in Kempo Subdistrict, Dompu Regency. The study employed a descriptive quantitative approach based on Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Secondary data used included land cover, rainfall, slope gradient, soil type, and administrative boundaries. Analysis was conducted through classification, scoring, weighting, and parameter overlay using QGIS. The results of the study show changes in land cover during the observation period, particularly an increase in the area of dryland agriculture from 7,594.37 ha in 2017 to 9,729.13 ha in 2021, while scrubland decreased from 3,029.54 ha to 1,382.39 ha. Landslide risk mapping identified three classes: low, moderate, and high. High-risk zones are primarily associated with hilly areas, steep to very steep slopes, Lithosol soils, relatively high rainfall, and land cover that has been converted to agricultural or open land. These results can serve as supporting information for land management and landslide mitigation in Kempo Subdistrict. Field validation and data alignment are necessary to improve the accuracy of the results.

papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. Understanding the interactions between hydrological, geological, and climatic factors governing landslide dam evolution is crucial for hazard management planning. The Tairāwhiti Gisborne region on the East Coast of Aotearoa New Zealand is prone to landslides and subsequent dams, due to its steep slopes, susceptible lithology, and exposure to tropical storms from the east. Despite this vulnerability, very little is known about the material properties and behaviour of landslide dams in this area. The primary aim of this thesis was to investigate the geomorphic and geotechnical aspects of dams in the Tairāwhiti Gisborne region, to understand their formation and breach processes. Two large landslide dams were chosen as case studies, the 1,485,500 m3 Waiorongomai Landslide Dam which formed in the north of the region in early January 2023, and the 98,500 m3 Tiniroto Landslide Dam which formed in the south of the region on the 3rd of October 2023. Three elements of analyses were used to investigate these landslide dams. First, historic landslides were mapped in the two catchments, to investigate the rate of landslide-river connectivity and landslide dam frequency. Each landslide source and deposit were mapped as polygons, using aerial imagery between 1988 and 2023. Second, the short-term evolution of the Waiorongomai and Tiniroto landslide dams was documented through a series of engineering geomorphic maps, using LiDAR and aerial imagery in ArcGIS Pro. papers.summary: Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are rapid slope failures within shallow soil layers, generally less than 2 m thick, that are triggered by intense or prolonged rainfall on steep soilmantled slopes.NASA's Global Landslide Catalog recorded 11,033 reported rainfall-triggered landslides during 2007-2019, and an overlay with the FAO land-cover map indicated that up to 80% occurred in vegetated land-cover types.These observations show that vegetation does not uniformly prevent landslides.Its stabilizing effect has conventionally been represented mainly as additional root cohesion, although rainfall-induced instability is controlled by interactions among precipitation, hydrological responses, root-system architecture, soil depth, and the potential failure zone.Roots can increase mechanical resistance while also modifying infiltration, preferential flow, runoff, soil-water redistribution, saturation, and pore-waterpressure development.Consequently, the same root system can reinforce shallow soil but promote hydrological weakening where water is transferred beneath the principal rooting zone.

papers.summary: Regional Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) are essential tools for predicting rainfall-induced slope instability across broad geographic regions. papers.title: Development of an AI-Driven Model to Predict Slope Collapse Due to Rainfall
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: This doctoral research explored the application of Geographic Information System (GIS) and Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) techniques to improve soil mapping processes and support land management and biodiversity conservation, in alignment with the objectives of the National Biodiversity Future Center (NBFC). The study was conducted in two Regional Parks of the Northern Apennines, a region characterized by high environmental heterogeneity and a rich cartographic heritage. papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
authors: , Dr. Annisa Trisnia Sasmi, S.Si., M.T
papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Each parameter was assigned a score and weight, followed by an overlay process to generate a landslide susceptibility map. Validation was conducted using 85 landslide occurrence points from 2025, obtained from the Wonogiri Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), with 12 of these points verified through field surveys. The results indicate that landslide susceptibility is categorized into four classes: low, moderate, high, and very high. The moderate susceptibility class covers the largest area. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

papers.summary: (English) Hydro-geomorphological hazards such as floods and rainfall-induced landslides frequently co-occur in mountainous regions, driven by shared meteorological forcing but governed by distinct hydrological and geotechnical mechanisms. Improving their anticipation requires modelling frameworks capable of consistently representing subsurface hydrological conditioning and its interaction with transient triggering processes. This thesis develops and evaluates a physically based, forecast-driven multi-hazard modelling framework for early warning applications in the Upper Garonne River Basin (Val d’Aran, Central Pyrenees, Spain). The research progresses through three interconnected stages. First, an event-based slope stability model is enhanced through a novel multi-objective calibration strategy that explicitly represents both antecedent and final slope stability conditions. Results demonstrate that inadequate representation of subsurface hydrological states leads to physically inconsistent pre-event instability, highlighting the sensitivity of slope response to antecedent moisture conditions. Therefore, this study aims to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the engineering geology properties of the Muriwai Awhitu Group sands to gain more appreciation for the complexity of this geological unit and the Muriwai slope conditions. Field investigations were undertaken to characterise landslide morphology and collect representative soil samples for laboratory testing. Physical, mineralogical, and geochemical analyses were combined with geotechnical characterisation and slope stability modelling using Factor of Safety (FoS) analyses to evaluate the mechanisms responsible for failure. papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslides are a common natural disaster in areas with steep topography, including Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict, Lembata Regency, East Nusa Tenggara. This disaster is caused by a combination of natural factors, such as high rainfall, slope gradients, soil types, and human activities that alter land use. This study aims to analyze the landslide susceptibility levels and identify mitigation efforts in Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict. This research employed a descriptive method with a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. The data used included slope gradient maps, soil type maps, rainfall data, and land use maps, analyzed using a weighted overlay technique to produce a landslide susceptibility map. Primary data were collected through field observations, while secondary data were obtained from relevant agencies such as BPBD and PUPR of Lembata Regency. The results show that the landslide susceptibility levels in Ile Ape Timur are categorized into four classes: not susceptible (3,174 hectares), less susceptible (25 hectares), susceptible (718 hectares), and highly susceptible (6 hectares). The main factors influencing susceptibility are steep slopes, Andosols soil prone to erosion, and relatively high annual rainfall. Recommended mitigation efforts include structural approaches, such as terracing and the installation of early warning systems (EWS), as well as non-structural approaches, including community education and disaster simulations. This study is expected to serve as a basis for the government and local communities to implement effective landslide disaster mitigation measures, minimizing material losses and casualties.

papers.title: Understanding the rainfall triggering post-fire debris flows in California
papers.summary: Post-fire debris flows (PFDFs) are a cascading hazard resulting from the interaction between intense rainfall and susceptible terrain altered by wildfire. These events have proven devastating in the past, damaging infrastructure and communities, particularly in California, where fire season in the warm months is closely followed by rainfall during the cool season. Consequently, this dissertation integrates multiple datasets and methods to characterize rainfall and atmospheric conditions associated with storms triggering post-fire debris flows, providing new insight into the rainfall environments, precipitation-system structure, predictive controls, and future changes in PFDF hazard across California. papers.title: Surface Soil Moisture in Challenging Environments: Methodological Advances and Drought Monitoring Applications

papers.title: Development of an advanced computational approach for early warning and predictions of rainfall-induced slope failures
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most common natural hazards, threatening lives, homes, and infrastructure worldwide. This research develops a novel approach to predict landslides and provide early warning, even when field data are limited. The study creates advanced computer models that represent real soil conditions and simulate how slopes respond to heavy rainfall. These physics-based models are then combined with machine learning that learn continuously from monitoring data, allowing predictions to be updated and refined over time. By improving prediction accuracy, this research supports more effective landslide early warning systems and helps reduce damage and loss of life.

Roads interrupt these controls by compressing peat and blocking lateral groundwater flow, producing persistent changes in water-table position, oxygen exposure, solute movement, and decomposition. As road removal and peatland reclamation become more common, restoration must be guided by how disturbance continues to affect ecosystem function below ground, rather than only whether vegetation or surface hydrology appear to recover. Road loading compressed and displaced peat horizons, while reduced hydraulic conductivity beneath the road divided the site into wetter upgradient and drier downgradient zones. These hydrological contrasts were consistent with differences in nutrient transport, ionic conditions, and decomposition patterns. Because subsurface compression can persist after mineral fill is removed, restoration planning must address both lateral hydrological reconnection and the altered vertical arrangement of peat that controls water storage, redox conditions, and substrate availability. DNA-based methods can identify microbial responses before visible ecosystem recovery, but only when extraction differences reflect biological conditions rather than peat chemistry. papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Plant roots play a crucial role in maintaining soil health by influencing physical structure and hydraulic properties. This study investigates relationships between root morphology of wheat genotypes and their impacts on soil structure and hydraulic characteristics. Using shovelomics, we characterized root systems of wheat cultivars (Paragon, Bologna) and landraces (Senatore-Cappelli, Watkins238) selected for contrasting root morphologies. X-ray computed tomography (CT) was applied to examine soil pore networks at cylinder and aggregate scales, while soil hydraulic properties were measured using Wind evaporation and dew point techniques. Results demonstrated significant genotype-driven differences in soil morphology and hydraulic functions. Structural analyses (Minkowski functionals, percolation theory) showed significant variability in bioporosity and pore connectivity among genotypes compared to bare soil. Senatore-Cappelli exhibited notably larger biopores (>1 mm diameter). Hydraulic characterization using a van Genuchten bimodal model revealed statistically significant differences in soil water retention curves and hydraulic conductivity among genotypes. Root traits, including total root length, branching frequency, lateral root length, and root diameter, significantly correlated with soil pore size distribution and hydraulic parameters. This analysis underscores the importance of root architecture in modulating soil structure and water dynamics, highlighting the potential of specific wheat genotypes to affect soil health, water retention, and agricultural sustainability.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF DOLOMITE AMENDMENTS ON PER- AND POLYFLUOROALKYL SUBSTANCES (PFAS) LEACHING IN AGRICULTURAL SOILS
papers.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are often found in agricultural soils due to land application of biosolids, wastewater-derived materials, and atmospheric deposition. However, PFAS transport behavior in variably saturated agricultural soils remains poorly studied. This study evaluates PFAS mobility within unsaturated soil using both intact soil cores (diameter: 3 inches, referred to as large columns (LC)) and packed, homogeneous soil columns (diameter: 1 inch, referred to as small columns (SC)) under the presence and absence of dolomite, which was recently reported to be able to reduce PFAS mobility through adsorption. All columns were amended with a biosolid (Milorganite) and half of the large and small columns received a powdered dolomite amendment at the surface. Columns were subjected to episodic infiltration based on precipitation data from 2019, and the leachate was collected at the base of each column for PFAS analysis. Our results showed that (1) the leaching of PFAS was strongly dependent on the structure and properties of the PFAS, and (2) dolomite amendments could lower the leaching of PFAS. The findings from this research will improve our quantitative understanding of how PFAS move through agricultural soils and the potential risks associated with land application, as well as the design and implementation of science-based management practices and regulation frameworks.

papers.title: Understanding preferential water flow and its contribution to inrush hazard susceptibility in block cave mining : an integrated modelling approach
papers.summary: Water infiltration dynamics in block cave mining are critical to understanding and managing inrush hazards that threaten mine safety and operational continuity. Primary water sources, groundwater aquifers, water-bearing faults, and surface water entering through the subsidence crater interact within the cave muck pile through preferential flow pathways that develop and evolve during mining. How that water then partitions within the broken ore column has received less attention. papers.summary: Understanding subsurface water movement, particularly preferential water flow, is critical for water resource management and predicting contaminant transport. However, traditional invasive methods like dye staining experiments are destructive and only provide static information. Consequently, this thesis investigates the effectiveness of 3D time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) for monitoring infiltration dynamics on a forested hillslope in Lower Austria. papers.summary: Conventional barrier systems in tailings storage facilities often rely on thick monolithic geomaterials (1.5 m-2.5 m) or geosynthetics that fail under ex-treme precipitation or snowmelt events typical in Nordic climates. This study proposes and evaluates a novel, fully unsaturated multi-layered cover system (MLCS) constructed majorly from on-site sourced tailings and waste rock. The tailings are modified through either mixing with biochar and clay or by altering surface polarity to make them functional components of a newly conceptual-ized MLCS. The MLCS design integrates capillary barrier mechanisms with a water-entry-head-controlled hydrophobic interface to act as a final hydraulic buffer during extreme ponding conditions. Laboratory characterization of soil-water retention curves (SWRCs), unsaturated hydraulic conductivity functions (SHCFs), and hydrophobicity confirmed the enhanced water-buffering capaci-ty of the modified tailings mixtures. Especially, the threshold-based break-through resistance of the hydrophobic layer (WEH ≈ 4.71 kPa) allowed the construction of an overall thin MLCS (≤0.5-m-thick). This MLCS was physically modelled in an instrumented 1-D column subjected to a ponding head equivalent to a 500-year rainfall event. Results showed complete suppression of percolation below the MLCS for 61 days of testing period, with the hydro-phobic layer preventing breakthrough even after upper layers neared saturation. Complementary two-stage finite element simulations, incorporating WEH-triggered hydraulic switching, accurately reproduced observed suction, water-content, and percolation behaviour. The findings demonstrate that the proposed MLCS provides a climate-resilient, all-weather hydraulic barrier, reduces dependence on imported materials, and offers a feasible, low-cost closure strategy for Nordic TSFs. Further work should assess performance under field-scale slopes including lateral drainage conditions.
